110711.e: In a serious accident, radioactive iodine could be released. The tablets fill the thyroid gland with normal iodine beforehand, so it hardly takes in the radioactive kind.
110711.m: Iodine tablets protect the thyroid gland in a nuclear accident.

110712.q: Which radioactive gas from the ground can collect in cellars, especially in the Alps and the Jura?
110712.e: Radon forms when uranium in the ground decays. The Federal Office of Public Health recommends ventilating or sealing houses well in affected areas.
110712.m: Radon is a radioactive gas from the ground.

a: Yes, it makes a quiet hum
110713.e: Radioactive radiation is invisible, odourless and silent. Only special measuring devices can detect it.
110713.m: You can't see, smell or hear radioactive radiation.

110714.q: What does the sign with three black blades around a dot on a yellow background warn of?
110714.e: The radiation warning sign shows a dot with three blades. It marks places and containers with radioactive substances.
110714.m: The yellow trefoil sign warns of radioactivity.

110715.q: Where does a large part of the natural radiation everyone receives come from?
a: From the ground, rocks and space
110715.e: Radiation comes from natural radioactive substances in the ground and from cosmic radiation. Our bodies also contain small amounts of radioactive substances.
110715.m: Natural radiation is all around us.

110716.q: In which reactor accident in 1986 did radioactive substances reach Switzerland?
110716.e: After the explosion at the Chernobyl nuclear power station in what is now Ukraine, a radioactive cloud drifted over Europe. Ticino in particular had radioactive rain.
110716.m: The Chernobyl accident in 1986 also affected Switzerland.

110717.q: What electric charge does an alpha particle have?
110717.e: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus without its electron shell. Its charge is therefore positive and twice as large as that of a proton.
110717.m: Alpha particles carry a double positive charge.

110718.q: How does the atomic number of a nucleus change in alpha decay?
110718.e: With the alpha particle, the nucleus loses two protons. This produces an element two places further forward in the periodic table.
110718.m: In alpha decay, the element moves two places forward.

110719.q: Roughly how far does alpha radiation travel in air?
110719.e: Alpha particles keep colliding with air molecules and are quickly slowed down. After a few centimetres they are stopped.
110719.m: Alpha particles only travel a few centimetres in air.

110720.q: Why is an alpha emitter especially dangerous if it is breathed in or swallowed?
a: It gives all its energy to cells in a tiny space
It heats the whole body strongly
It creates electric current in the blood
110720.e: If the substance is breathed in or swallowed, it lies right next to living cells. The particles damage them very badly over a short distance.
110720.m: Alpha emitters inside the body are very harmful.

110721.q: Uranium-238 emits an alpha particle. What is the mass number of the new nucleus?
110721.e: An alpha particle takes 4 nuclear particles with it. 238 minus 4 = 234, producing thorium-234.
110721.m: In alpha decay, the mass number falls by four.

110722.q: Where does alpha radiation come from?
a: From radioactive substances such as uranium
110722.e: Alpha radiation is produced when the nuclei of radioactive substances decay. Uranium and radon are examples.
110722.m: Alpha radiation comes from radioactive substances.

110723.q: In which device can you see alpha particles as short, thick trails of mist?
110723.e: In a cloud chamber the air is supersaturated with alcohol vapour. Flying particles leave trails of droplets like vapour trails.
110723.m: A cloud chamber makes particle tracks visible.

110724.q: What can already block alpha radiation?
110724.e: Alpha particles are large and are quickly slowed down. Even a sheet of paper or the skin stops them.
110724.m: A sheet of paper stops alpha radiation.

110725.q: What does beta-minus radiation consist of?
110725.e: In beta-minus decay, the nucleus shoots out an electron at high speed.
110725.m: Beta radiation consists of fast electrons.

110726.q: What happens in the nucleus during beta-minus decay?
a: A neutron turns into a proton
A proton vanishes without a trace
The nucleus splits into two halves
110726.e: A neutron becomes a proton, an electron and an antineutrino. The electron leaves the nucleus as beta radiation.
110726.m: In beta decay, a neutron becomes a proton.

110727.e: Beta particles go through paper but are stopped by a few millimetres of metal.
110727.m: A thin metal sheet helps against beta radiation.

110728.q: Carbon-14 undergoes beta-minus decay. Which nucleus is formed?
110728.e: The atomic number rises from 6 to 7, the mass number stays 14. The element with atomic number 7 is nitrogen.
110728.m: Carbon-14 becomes nitrogen-14 through beta decay.

110729.q: Roughly how far does beta radiation travel in air?
110729.e: Electrons are light and small and hit air molecules less often. So they travel up to a few metres.
110729.m: Beta radiation travels a few metres in air.

110730.q: Where does beta radiation get its name from?
a: From the second letter of the Greek alphabet
From the Latin word for light
110730.e: The types of radiation were named in order with Greek letters: alpha, beta and gamma.
110730.m: Alpha, beta and gamma are Greek letters.

110731.q: Which particle does a nucleus emit in beta-plus decay?
110731.e: In beta-plus decay, a proton becomes a neutron. This produces a positron, the positively charged counterpart of the electron.

110732.q: What is beta radiation used for in factories, for example when making paper or plastic film?
110732.e: The thicker the film, the fewer beta particles get through. A measuring device behind the film thus monitors the thickness.
110732.m: Beta radiation can be used to check the thickness of films.

110733.e: Like light and X-rays, gamma radiation is an electromagnetic wave. But it has a particularly large amount of energy.
110733.m: Gamma radiation is very high-energy light that we can't see.

110734.q: What is the best shield against gamma radiation?
a: Thick layers of lead or concrete
110734.e: Gamma radiation is very penetrating. Dense, heavy substances such as lead weaken it best.
110734.m: Against gamma radiation you need lead or thick concrete.

110735.q: Does a nucleus become a different element by giving off gamma radiation?
a: No, the numbers of protons and neutrons stay the same
Yes, it always loses a proton
110735.e: With gamma radiation, the nucleus only gives off extra energy. Its make-up stays unchanged.
110735.m: Gamma radiation does not change the element.

110736.q: What is gamma radiation often used for in medicine?
110736.e: Gamma radiation kills bacteria and viruses, even through the packaging. This is how disposable syringes are sterilised.
110736.m: Gamma radiation can sterilise medical equipment.

110737.q: Why must you protect yourself from strong gamma radiation?
a: It can damage cells in the body
110737.e: Gamma radiation goes deep into the body and can damage cells and their genetic material there.
110737.m: Strong gamma radiation is dangerous for the body.

110738.q: Which radiation has the shorter wavelength?
110738.e: The shorter the wavelength, the more energy the radiation carries. Gamma radiation has the shortest wavelengths of all electromagnetic waves.
110738.m: Gamma radiation has very short wavelengths.

110739.q: What is the so-called Gamma Knife used for in hospitals?
a: For targeted radiation of brain tumours
110739.e: Many weak gamma rays are focused on one point from different directions. There they destroy the diseased tissue without any need for surgery.
110739.m: Focused gamma rays can treat brain tumours.

110740.q: Can you see gamma radiation with your eyes?
110740.e: Gamma radiation is an electromagnetic wave like light, but outside the visible range. You need measuring devices such as a Geiger counter.

110741.q: What does the half-life tell you?
a: The time after which half of the nuclei have decayed
Half the lifetime of a single atom
The time until all nuclei have decayed
The length of half an hour
110741.e: After one half-life, half of the original nuclei are left. After another half-life, half of those again.
110741.m: After each half-life, half is left.

110742.q: A sample contains 800 radioactive nuclei with a half-life of 10 minutes. How many are left after 40 minutes?
110742.e: 40 minutes are four half-lives. 800, then 400, 200, 100 and finally 50 nuclei.
110742.m: With each half-life the number of nuclei halves.

110743.q: After how many half-lives is only about a thousandth of the nuclei left?
110743.e: Halving ten times gives 1/1024, so about a thousandth. That is why a substance is considered largely decayed after about ten half-lives.
110743.m: Ten half-lives leave only about a thousandth.

110744.q: Can you predict exactly when a single radioactive nucleus will decay?
a: No, only the probability is known
Yes, always after exactly one half-life
110744.e: Radioactive decay is a random process. Only with very many nuclei do you get the regular halving.
110744.m: The decay of a single nucleus is random.

110745.q: Iodine-131 has a half-life of about 8 days. How much of 64 mg of iodine-131 is left after 24 days?
110745.e: 24 days are three half-lives. 64 mg, then 32 mg, then 16 mg, then 8 mg.
110745.m: Short half-lives make a substance decay quickly.

110746.q: Roughly how long is the half-life of uranium-238?
110746.e: Uranium-238 decays extremely slowly, with a half-life of about 4.5 billion years. That is about the age of the Earth.

110747.q: What happens to the half-life of a radioactive substance if you heat it strongly?
110747.e: Nuclear decay is practically unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical reactions. The half-life is a fixed property of each isotope.

110748.q: What is a Geiger counter used for?
110748.e: A Geiger counter registers single particles of radiation. This shows whether something is radiating and how strongly.
110748.m: A Geiger counter detects radioactive radiation.

110749.q: What was the profession of Hans Geiger, after whom the Geiger counter is named?
110749.e: Hans Geiger was a German physicist. He worked for some years with Ernest Rutherford in England.
110749.m: The Geiger counter is named after the physicist Hans Geiger.

110750.q: How does a Geiger counter make radiation audible?
a: With a click for each particle detected
110750.e: Each particle detected in the counter tube creates a short pulse of current. A loudspeaker turns this into a click.
110750.m: Each click of a Geiger counter means one particle detected.

110751.q: What is inside the tube of a Geiger counter?
110751.e: The radiation ionises the gas in the tube. Because of the high voltage, an avalanche of charges forms, which is measured as a pulse.
110751.m: In the counter tube, radiation briefly makes the gas conduct.

110752.q: Why does a Geiger counter click now and then even when there is no radiation source nearby?
a: It measures the natural background radiation
It measures the radiation from a mobile phone
It reacts to the room temperature
110752.e: There is weak natural radiation everywhere. It is called the background count and must be subtracted from measurements.
110752.m: A Geiger counter always shows background radiation too.

110753.q: What do you call the number of pulses a Geiger counter measures per unit of time?
110753.e: The count rate is given, for example, in pulses per minute. The higher it is, the stronger the radiation at that spot.
110753.m: The count rate shows how many particles are measured per unit of time.

110754.q: How does the count rate change when you move the Geiger counter away from a radiation source?
110754.e: As the distance grows, the radiation spreads over a larger area. So fewer particles hit the counter tube.
110754.m: Distance is good protection against radiation.

110755.q: What does it mean when a Geiger counter clicks very quickly one after another?
110755.e: Each click stands for one particle detected. The faster it clicks, the stronger the radiation.

110756.q: What is a “keystone species” in an ecosystem?
a: A species on which many others depend
The largest species in the area
The rarest species in the area
110756.e: A keystone species strongly shapes its habitat. The beaver, for example, dams streams and so creates habitat for many other species.
110756.m: Many other species depend on a keystone species.

110757.q: What do the two parts of the word “biodiversity” mean?
110757.e: “Bio” comes from the Greek word for life, “diversity” from the Latin word for variety. The term was made famous by the biologist Edward O. Wilson.
110757.m: Biodiversity means the variety of life.

110758.q: Which international treaty to protect biological diversity was signed at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro?
110758.e: The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) was opened for signature at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. Switzerland is also a party to it.
110758.m: The 1992 Convention on Biological Diversity protects biological diversity worldwide.

110759.q: Which goal was set in 2022 in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework?
a: To protect 30 percent of the area
110759.e: By 2030, at least 30 percent of the Earth's land and sea areas are to be effectively protected. This goal is also called “30 by 30”.
110759.m: By 2030, 30 percent of the Earth's surface is to be protected.

a: The benefits of nature for people
110760.e: Ecosystem services are things nature does that we benefit from, such as pollination, clean drinking water or fertile soil.
110760.m: Nature provides services for us such as pollination and clean water.

110761.q: What is the International Day for Biological Diversity for?
a: To draw attention to protecting the variety of species
110761.e: The UN declared 22 May the Day for Biological Diversity. On this day, people should think about protecting animals, plants and habitats.
110761.m: 22 May is the Day for Biological Diversity.

110762.q: Which federal office in Switzerland is mainly responsible for protecting biodiversity?
110762.e: The Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN) is responsible for protecting nature and the landscape. For example, it publishes Switzerland's Red Lists.
110762.m: The FOEN looks after biodiversity in Switzerland.

110763.q: What are areas of the Earth called that have especially many species and are also under great threat?
110763.e: Biodiversity hotspots are regions with very many species, often found nowhere else, whose original habitats have already shrunk a lot. Examples are Madagascar or the Mediterranean region.
110763.m: Hotspots are areas rich in species and also under threat.

110764.q: Which habitat on land is considered the richest in species on Earth?
110764.e: In tropical rainforests, especially many species live in a small area. The reasons are warmth, moisture and a stable climate.
110764.m: The tropical rainforest is the habitat on land with the most species.

110765.q: Which group of animals has the most known species?
110765.e: More than half of all described animal species are insects. Beetles alone have several hundred thousand species.
110765.m: Insects are the group of animals with the most species.

110766.q: Roughly how does the variety of species change as you go from the poles towards the equator?
110766.e: Towards the equator, the number of species usually rises clearly. Warmth and lots of solar energy favour great variety.
110766.m: The variety of species increases towards the equator.

110767.q: Roughly how many species have been scientifically described worldwide?
110767.e: So far, around two million species have been described. Experts think there are many more species still undiscovered.
110767.m: Around two million species have been described, and many more are still unknown.

110768.q: Which sea habitat is considered especially rich in species and is often called the “rainforest of the sea”?
110768.e: Coral reefs cover only a tiny part of the sea floor, but they are home to a large share of all sea species.
110768.m: Coral reefs are the rainforests of the sea.

110769.q: Which meadows are among the habitats richest in species in Switzerland?
110769.e: Poor, dry meadows are not fertilised. Many different flowers grow there, which in turn give food to many insects.
110769.m: Poor dry meadows are especially rich in species.

110770.q: What is a species called that has been brought to a new area by humans and pushes out native species there?
110770.e: Invasive species spread a lot and threaten native species. In Switzerland, for example, Himalayan balsam is an invasive alien plant.
110770.m: Invasive species push out native species.

110771.q: What is the name of an invasive plant from North America that often grows on railway embankments in Switzerland and has golden-yellow flowers?
110771.e: Canadian goldenrod forms dense patches and pushes out native plants. In Switzerland it is considered an invasive alien plant.
110771.m: Canadian goldenrod is an invasive alien plant.

a: Differences in genetic material within a species
110772.e: Genetic diversity means that the individuals of a species differ in their genes. That is why, for example, not all roe deer are the same.
110772.m: Genetic diversity means differences in genetic material within a species.

110773.q: Why is high genetic diversity important for a species?
110773.e: The more varied the genetic material, the more likely it is that some individuals can cope with diseases or changes in the climate. This lets the species survive.
110773.m: Genetic diversity helps species to adapt to changes.

110774.q: Why are most bananas sold in shops almost genetically identical?
a: They only grow in one country
They are mixed in a laboratory
They have no genes at all
110774.e: The common Cavendish variety is grown from offshoots, so the plants are clones. That is why a fungal disease can threaten whole plantations.
110774.m: Clones without genetic diversity are vulnerable to disease.

110775.q: What is the seed vault on Svalbard for?
a: It stores seeds of crop plants as a reserve
It stores oil for the winter
It measures the temperature at the North Pole
110775.e: Seeds from all over the world are stored in the permafrost on Svalbard. If varieties are lost elsewhere, there is a backup copy here.
110775.m: Seeds are stored in the Svalbard vault as a reserve for the world.

110776.q: What can happen when an animal population is made up of only very few animals?
a: Inbreeding and greater risk of disease
110776.e: When there are only a few animals, they are often closely related. Genetic diversity falls, and inherited diseases or epidemics can have a bigger effect.

110777.q: Which disaster in the 19th century shows how dangerous it can be to grow only a few varieties of potato?
110777.e: From 1845, potato blight destroyed large parts of the harvest in Ireland. Because the same varieties were grown almost everywhere, the disease spread unchecked.
110777.m: Growing only a few varieties makes harvests vulnerable to disease.

110778.q: Which big cat is known for its remarkably low genetic diversity?
110778.e: Cheetahs are genetically very similar, probably because their numbers fell sharply in the past. This makes them more vulnerable to disease.
110778.m: The cheetah has only low genetic diversity.

110779.q: Why are wildlife corridors or wildlife bridges important for genetic diversity?
110779.e: Animals can travel between separate areas using corridors and bridges. This mixes populations and keeps genetic diversity.
110779.m: Wildlife bridges link populations with each other.

110780.q: Which organisation publishes the worldwide Red List of Threatened Species?
110780.e: The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) draws up the worldwide Red List. It assesses how threatened species of animals, plants and fungi are.
110780.m: The IUCN publishes the worldwide Red List.

110781.q: In which country does the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) have its headquarters?
110781.e: The IUCN is based in Gland in the canton of Vaud on Lake Geneva. It was founded in 1948.
110781.m: The IUCN has its headquarters in Switzerland.

110783.q: Which category of the Red List means the highest threat to a species that is still alive?
110783.e: From low to high, the order is: least concern, near threatened, vulnerable, endangered, critically endangered. After that come only the categories for extinct species.
110783.m: “Critically endangered” is the highest level of threat.

110784.q: What does the category “extinct in Switzerland” mean?
a: The species is missing here but lives elsewhere
The species no longer lives anywhere
110784.e: A species can have disappeared from Switzerland but still be found in other countries. This is called regionally extinct.
110784.m: Regionally extinct species still live in other countries.

110785.q: What does the category “near threatened” mean on the Red List?
a: Soon threatened if nothing is done
110785.e: Near threatened species only just fail to meet the criteria for “threatened”. But without protection they could soon slip into a higher category.
110785.m: Near threatened species are close to being threatened.

110786.q: Which category is given when too little is known about a species?
110786.e: If there are no observations or counts, the threat cannot be assessed. The species is then put in the category “data deficient”.
110786.m: If data are missing, the threat cannot be assessed.

110787.q: Ideally, how often are Red Lists revised?
110787.e: Populations are always changing. That is why Red Lists are reassessed regularly so that they stay up to date.

110788.q: What does the international agreement CITES regulate?
a: Trade in endangered animals and plants
110788.e: CITES is the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species, also known as the Washington Convention. It bans or limits trade in thousands of animal and plant species.
110788.m: CITES protects endangered species from trade.

110789.q: Why are you not allowed to bring ivory souvenirs into Switzerland?
a: Trade in ivory is banned to protect elephants
Ivory is only found in museums
110789.e: Elephants are poached for their ivory. That is why trade in it is banned under the CITES agreement, and customs officers confiscate such souvenirs.
110789.m: Souvenirs made from protected animals are banned.

110790.q: Why are elephants and rhinos poached?
110790.e: The ivory of the tusks and the horn of rhinos are sold illegally for a lot of money. Poaching is a major threat to these animals.
110790.m: Poaching for ivory and horn threatens elephants and rhinos.

110791.q: Which amphibian with green skin and sticky toe pads is endangered in Switzerland?
110791.e: The European tree frog needs warm ponds without fish. Many such ponds have disappeared, which is why it is endangered.
110791.m: The tree frog needs warm ponds without fish.

110792.q: Which large forest bird is highly endangered in Switzerland and is very sensitive to disturbance from winter sports?
110792.e: The capercaillie lives in open mountain forests. Being disturbed in winter costs it a lot of energy, and suitable forests have become rare.
110792.m: The capercaillie is an endangered forest bird.

110793.q: Which orchid with a yellow, shoe-shaped flower is protected in Switzerland?
110793.e: The yellow lady's slipper is one of the largest native orchids. It must not be picked or dug up.
110793.m: The lady's slipper is a protected orchid.

110794.q: Which great ape lives in the mountain forests of the Virunga volcanoes in Africa and is highly endangered?
110794.e: Mountain gorillas are now found only in a few mountain forests in Rwanda, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Thanks to strict protection, their numbers are slowly rising again.
110794.m: The mountain gorilla lives only in a few African mountain forests.

110795.q: How does the destruction of rainforest threaten orangutans?
110795.e: Orangutans live in trees on Borneo and Sumatra. When forests are cleared for plantations, they lose food and shelter.
110795.m: Without rainforest, orangutans have no habitat.

110796.q: What happened to the moas, giant flightless birds of New Zealand, after people settled on the islands?
110796.e: Some moas were over three metres tall. After the Maori settled New Zealand, they were wiped out within a few centuries.
110796.m: New Zealand's moas were wiped out by humans.

110797.q: Why did the passenger pigeon, once the most common bird in North America, die out?
a: Because of too many enemies in the sea
110797.e: Passenger pigeons were hunted in their millions. The last one, called Martha, died in a zoo in 1914.
110797.m: The passenger pigeon died out in 1914, even though it was once very common.

110798.q: Which marsupial, also called the Tasmanian tiger, has been considered extinct since the last zoo animal died in 1936?
110798.e: The thylacine had a striped back end and in the end lived only on Tasmania. The last known animal died in 1936 in Hobart Zoo.
110798.m: The thylacine has been extinct since 1936.

110799.q: Which wild ox, the ancestor of our domestic cattle, died out in Poland in 1627?
110799.e: The last female aurochs died in Poland in 1627. Domestic cattle are descended from the aurochs.
110799.m: The aurochs is the ancestor of domestic cattle.

110800.q: Which wild animal was wiped out in Switzerland from 1904 and has been returning from Italy now and then since 2005?
110800.e: The last native bear was shot in the Lower Engadine in 1904. Since 2005, single bears have been coming in again from Italy.
110800.m: The bear was wiped out in Switzerland from 1904.

110801.q: Why was Steller's sea cow wiped out only about 27 years after it was discovered?
a: Seafarers hunted it for its meat
It froze in a harsh winter
It could no longer find food
110801.e: Steller's sea cow lived in the Bering Sea. Seafarers hunted it so much that it disappeared around 1768.
110801.m: Steller's sea cow was wiped out in a short time.

110802.q: What is a main reason why animal species on islands die out especially easily?
110802.e: Island species often do not know enemies such as rats, cats or pigs. If such animals are brought in, the island species have hardly any protection.
110802.m: Enemies brought in from elsewhere are a special threat to island species.

110803.q: Which bird of today did the great auk of the North Atlantic, wiped out in 1844, look like?
110803.e: The great auk was large, flightless and black and white like a penguin. The last known birds were killed off Iceland in 1844.
110803.m: The great auk was wiped out in 1844.

110804.q: What is Info Flora responsible for in Switzerland?
110804.e: Info Flora is the national data and information centre for the Swiss flora. It collects reports of wild plants that have been found.
110804.m: Info Flora collects data on Swiss plant life.

110805.q: Who can report plant finds to Info Flora?
a: Only members of the Federal Council
110805.e: Besides botanists, interested non-experts can also report what they see, for example with an app. The reports are checked.
110805.m: Non-experts can report plant finds too.

110806.q: Info Flora helps to draw up the Red List of plants. What does a Red List show?
110806.e: A Red List shows which animal or plant species are rare or threatened with extinction. Info Flora draws up the Red List of ferns and flowering plants on behalf of the federal government.
110806.m: A Red List shows which species are threatened.

110807.q: Which plants does Info Flora keep a special eye on because they push out native species?
110807.e: Info Flora keeps lists of invasive alien plants. Reports of finds help to fight their spread early.
110807.m: Info Flora monitors invasive alien plants.

110808.q: Which organisation in Switzerland collects data on wild animals, like Info Flora does for plants?
110808.e: info fauna is the national data and information centre for Swiss fauna, based in Neuchâtel. It collects sightings of animals such as amphibians, insects and mammals.
110808.m: info fauna collects data on wild animals.

110809.q: How can children help Info Flora too?
a: By pulling up plants and sending them in
By feeding animals at the zoo
110809.e: Experts and interested non-experts can report plant finds to Info Flora, for example with an app and a photo. This creates accurate maps of where plants grow.
110809.m: Everyone can report plant finds to Info Flora.

110810.q: Why are maps showing where plants grow useful for nature conservation?
a: They show changes in where species are found
110810.e: With many reports of finds over years, you can see where a species is declining or spreading. This helps to plan targeted measures.
110810.m: Distribution maps show where species are increasing or decreasing.

110811.q: Which institute in Sempach is the Swiss centre for data on birds?
110811.e: The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach in the canton of Lucerne studies and monitors the birds of Switzerland. It is a private, non-profit foundation.
110811.m: The Sempach Ornithological Institute collects data on birds.

a: A network of European protected areas
110812.e: The Emerald Network links areas that are important for threatened species and habitats in Europe.
110812.m: The Emerald Network is a network of European protected areas.

110813.q: Which international agreement from 1979 is the Emerald Network based on?
110813.e: The Bern Convention protects Europe's wild plants and animals and their habitats. It was signed in Bern in 1979.
110813.m: The Emerald Network is based on the Bern Convention.

110814.q: The Emerald Network is named after an emerald. What is an emerald?
110814.e: The emerald is a bright green gemstone. The green suits a network of valuable natural areas.
110814.m: An emerald is a green gemstone.

110815.q: Who works together in the Emerald Network?
a: Only the mountain railways of the Alps
110815.e: Many European countries take part in the Emerald Network, including countries outside the EU such as Switzerland. Together they protect important habitats.
110815.m: Many European countries are building the Emerald Network together.

110816.q: Why does Switzerland take part in the Emerald Network and not in Natura 2000?
a: It is not an EU member
110816.e: Natura 2000 only applies to EU countries. Through the Emerald Network, Switzerland can still link its important areas with the rest of Europe.
110816.m: As a non-EU country, Switzerland takes part in the Emerald Network.

110817.q: What is the aim of linking protected areas into a network across national borders?
110817.e: Many animals do not stick to borders. A network of protected areas allows exchange between populations and so protects variety.
110817.m: Linked protected areas help species to survive.

110818.q: What is the aim of the Bern Convention?
a: To protect Europe's wild animals and plants
To build more motorways across Europe
To allow hunting of all animals
110818.e: The Bern Convention was signed in Bern in 1979. It protects wild species and their habitats, and the Emerald Network is based on it.
110818.m: The Bern Convention protects Europe's nature.

110819.q: Which kinds of areas are added to the Emerald Network?
a: Areas with threatened species and habitats
110819.e: Areas are added that are important for species and habitats of European importance, for example bogs, floodplains or dry meadows.
110819.m: Valuable natural areas are added to the Emerald Network.

110820.q: What does the Swiss Biodiversity Strategy aim to achieve?
a: To preserve the variety of animals and plants
110820.e: The Federal Council adopted the Swiss Biodiversity Strategy. It sets out how the variety of species and habitats in Switzerland is to be preserved in the long term.
110820.m: The Swiss Biodiversity Strategy protects the variety of nature.

110822.q: What does the action plan for the Swiss Biodiversity Strategy describe?
110822.e: A strategy sets goals. The action plan then describes concrete measures for reaching these goals, for example new protected areas.
110822.m: The action plan puts the biodiversity strategy into practice with measures.

110823.q: What does the strategy mean by “ecological infrastructure”?
a: A network of protected and connecting areas
110823.e: The ecological infrastructure is made up of core areas and connecting areas. It is meant to give species enough habitat and routes to move along.
110823.m: The ecological infrastructure links habitats into a network.

110824.q: In Switzerland, who finally decides on a popular initiative, such as the biodiversity initiative of 2024?
a: The voters at the ballot box
110824.e: The people and the cantons vote on a popular initiative. The biodiversity initiative was rejected in September 2024, with around 63 percent voting no.
110824.m: Voters decide on popular initiatives at the ballot box.

110825.q: What is a biodiversity promotion area on a farm?
a: An area that leaves room for nature
110825.e: Farms leave part of their land in a natural state, for example as a meadow that is farmed lightly or as a hedge. In return they receive direct payments. At least 7 percent of the land is required.
110825.m: Biodiversity promotion areas give nature room on the farm.

110826.q: Apart from the federal government, which level is important for putting nature protection into practice in Switzerland?
110826.e: In Switzerland, nature protection is mainly a matter for the cantons. The federal government sets goals and helps with money and expertise.
110826.m: The cantons put nature protection into practice locally.

110827.q: Which goal does the strategy also pursue in built-up areas?
110827.e: Biodiversity is to be encouraged in towns and villages too, for example with flower meadows, hedges and green roofs.
110827.m: Nature is to be encouraged in built-up areas too.

110828.q: What have researchers found about flying insects in many parts of Europe over the last few decades?
a: There are far fewer insects than before
There are far more insects than before
The number has stayed exactly the same
Insects now only fly at night
110828.e: A well-known study from Germany found that flying insects in protected areas had declined by more than three quarters over 27 years. Many insect species are threatened in Switzerland too.
110828.m: The number of insects has fallen sharply.

110829.q: Why is the decline of insects a problem for farming?
110829.e: Many fruit trees and crops need insects for pollination. If bees, bumblebees and hoverflies are missing, harvests fall.
110829.m: Insects pollinate many of our crops.

110831.q: How does artificial lighting at night harm many insects?
a: It attracts them and wears them out
110831.e: Moths and other insects fly round lamps until they are exhausted or get eaten. This is called light pollution.
110831.m: Light pollution is a trap for night insects.

110832.q: Which substances from farming are considered one cause of the decline of insects?
110832.e: Pesticides such as insecticides can also kill or weaken useful insects. On top of that, flowers are lost through intensive farming.

110833.q: What can you do in your own garden against the decline of insects?
110833.e: Native flowers provide nectar and pollen. Dead wood, wild hedges and unmown corners also help insects.

110834.q: Why does a “bug hotel” mainly help wild bees?
a: It keeps them warm in winter
110834.e: Many wild bees lay their brood cells in hollow stems or drilled holes. A bug hotel offers such nesting places, but it only helps if there are flowers nearby.
110834.m: Bug hotels give wild bees places to nest.

110835.q: What effects does the decline of insects have on many birds?
110835.e: Many birds, such as swallows, feed themselves and their young on insects. If there are fewer insects, they find too little food.
110835.m: Fewer insects means less food for birds.

110836.q: What is considered one of the most important causes of the decline of biodiversity worldwide?
110836.e: When forests are cleared, wetlands are drained or land is built on, species lose their habitat. This is a main cause of the loss of species.
110836.m: Habitat loss is a main cause of species dying out.

110837.q: What is meant by soil sealing?
a: Soil is covered with tarmac or concrete
110837.e: Sealed soil can no longer take in water, and plants and soil animals can no longer find a home there.
110837.m: Sealed soil no longer supports life.

110838.q: Why do remote alpine pastures lose species when they are no longer used?
a: They become overgrown with bushes and then forest
110838.e: Without grazing or mowing, shrubs grow and later forest. Flowers that love light and their insects then disappear.
110838.m: Unused alpine pastures become overgrown and lose their variety of flowers.

110839.q: What is lost when old trees with holes are cut down?
a: Nesting holes for woodpeckers and owls
110839.e: Old trees with holes and dead wood are homes for woodpeckers, owls, bats and many beetles. Young trees only offer this after decades.
110839.m: Old trees are homes for many animals.

110840.q: Why are plants and animals in the high mountains losing habitat because of global warming?
a: They have to move higher up
110840.e: As temperatures rise, species that like the cold move to higher places. But there is less area higher up, and the summit is the end of the line.
110840.m: Mountain species move higher up as it gets warmer.

110841.q: What are especially large areas of rainforest cleared for in South East Asia?
110841.e: Large areas of rainforest in Indonesia and Malaysia are cleared for palm oil. Many animals and plants lose their habitat as a result.
110841.m: Palm oil plantations often replace rainforest.

110842.q: Why is draining bogs bad for nature?
110842.e: Bogs are home to specialised plants such as sundew and many rare insects. They also store a lot of carbon.
110842.m: Bogs are valuable habitats for specialists.

110843.q: What does it mean to revitalise a river?
110843.e: When it is revitalised, a straightened river gets more space, gravel banks and shallow banks again. This creates new habitats for fish, birds and insects.

110844.q: Which wild animal had been wiped out in Switzerland and was brought back from 1906 with animals from Italy?
110844.e: The ibex had been wiped out in Switzerland. From 1906, animals from the Gran Paradiso area in Italy were released, and the first ones were even smuggled in.
110844.m: The ibex was brought back from 1906.

110845.q: Which rodent was wiped out in Switzerland and brought back from 1956?
110845.e: The beaver had been wiped out in Switzerland by the beginning of the 19th century. Since 1956 it has been brought back and is spreading.
110845.m: The beaver returned to Switzerland after being brought back.

110846.q: Which wild cat was brought back to Switzerland from 1971?
110846.e: The lynx had been wiped out in Switzerland. From 1971, lynx were released in the Alps and later in the Jura.
110846.m: The lynx was brought back from 1971.

110847.q: What are amphibian fences along roads for in spring?
a: To get toads safely across the road
110847.e: Toads and frogs migrate to the water where they spawn in spring. Fences guide them into buckets, and helpers then carry them across the road.
110847.m: Amphibian fences save toads from traffic.

110848.q: What is meant by a conservation breeding programme in zoos?
110848.e: Zoos breed threatened species in a coordinated way so that a healthy reserve population is built up. Sometimes animals are later released into the wild.
110848.m: Zoos breed threatened species as a reserve.

110849.q: Which measure helps bats and swifts in towns and villages?
110849.e: Gaps and nooks are often lost when buildings are renovated. Special boxes and entrances give swifts and bats new places to stay.
110849.m: Nest boxes replace lost homes on buildings.

110850.q: Why do conservationists on the Central Plateau protect lapwing nests with markers and fences?
a: The nests are on the ground in fields
110850.e: Lapwings nest on the ground in meadows and fields. Marked and protected nests are spared by machines and foxes.
110850.m: Lapwings need protected nests on the ground.

110851.q: What are hedges of native shrubs for many animals?
110851.e: Hedges provide berries, insects as food and cover for birds, hedgehogs and weasels. They also link habitats in the open countryside.
110851.m: Hedges are valuable habitats in the countryside.

110852.q: What does it mean when a species is considered “extinct”?
a: Not a single individual is alive any more
110852.e: A species is considered extinct when not a single animal or plant can be found after a thorough search. Extinct species never come back.
110852.m: Extinct species are lost for ever.

110853.q: Which Red List category does a species get when it lives only in zoos or enclosures?
110853.e: If there are only animals left in human care, the species is considered “extinct in the wild”. For a long time, one example was Przewalski's horse, which was later released into the wild again.
110853.m: If a species lives only in zoos, it is extinct in the wild.

110854.q: Why do butterflies find little food in meadows that are often mown and heavily fertilised?
110854.e: Frequent mowing and fertilising favour a few fast-growing grasses. Flowers hardly get the chance to bloom, and caterpillars cannot find their food plants.
110854.m: Intensively farmed meadows offer butterflies hardly any flowers.

110855.q: What do experts use index fossils for?
a: To find out the depth of water today
110855.e: Index fossils appear only in layers from a particular period of time. If you find them, you know roughly how old the layer is.
110855.m: Index fossils give away the age of rock layers.

110856.q: Which feature must a good index fossil have?
a: It lived only a short time but was widespread
It lived in only one place
110856.e: A good index fossil was common, widespread and existed only during a short period of Earth's history. This lets layers be compared worldwide.
110856.m: Good index fossils were common, widespread and short-lived.

110857.q: Which extinct arthropods are important index fossils of the Palaeozoic era?
110857.e: Trilobites lived in the sea in the Palaeozoic and quickly developed into many species. That is why many of them are good index fossils.
110857.m: Trilobites are index fossils of the Palaeozoic.

110858.q: What is dating called in which you only say which layer is older or younger?
110858.e: Index fossils and the position of layers allow relative dating. An exact age in years only comes from an absolute method such as radioactive decay.

110859.q: Which sea animals with spiral shells are well-known index fossils from the time of the dinosaurs?
110859.e: Ammonites lived in the sea and quickly developed into many species. Their shells are also found in the Swiss Alps and the Jura.

110860.q: In undisturbed rock layers, where do the oldest layers usually lie?
110860.e: New layers are laid down on top of older ones. So the oldest lie at the bottom, unless the layers have been moved.
110860.m: The oldest layers lie at the bottom.

110861.q: Why are tiny fossils especially good for dating drill samples?
a: They are so common that they are found even in small samples
They are always made of gold
They still live in every sample today
110861.e: Tiny single-celled creatures with chalky shells, the foraminifera, occur in huge numbers. That is why they are found even in small drill cores, for example when searching for oil.
110861.m: Tiny fossils help to date drill samples.

110862.q: Why are land animals such as dinosaurs usually poorer index fossils than sea animals?
a: They lived too short a time
110862.e: In the sea, remains are quickly covered by mud and are often preserved. On land, dead bodies usually rot, so finds are rarer.
110862.m: Sea animals become fossils more often than land animals.

110863.q: What is especially important for a dead animal to become a fossil?
a: Being buried quickly away from air
Lying in the sun for a long time
110863.e: If a dead body is quickly covered by mud or sand, hardly any oxygen or scavengers can reach it. So hard parts are preserved and can turn to stone.
110863.m: Without quick burial, hardly any fossils form.

110864.q: Which parts of the body are most often preserved in fossils?
a: Hard parts such as bones and shells
110864.e: Hard parts break down slowly and become soaked with minerals. Soft parts are only preserved under very special conditions.
110864.m: Usually only the hard parts of a living thing turn to stone.

110865.q: In which fossil tree resin are insects often found perfectly preserved?
110865.e: Amber is fossilised resin from prehistoric trees. Insects caught in the sticky resin are preserved in it down to fine details.
110865.m: In amber, insects are preserved as if in a time capsule.

110867.q: What is the science that studies fossils called?
110867.e: Palaeontology studies living things from past ages of the Earth using fossils. Archaeology, on the other hand, studies traces of human cultures.

110868.q: What are species alive today that have hardly changed for millions of years, such as the coelacanth, called?
110868.e: The coelacanth was thought to be extinct until a living one was caught off South Africa in 1938. It looks very like its fossil relatives.
110868.m: Living fossils look very like their prehistoric relatives.

110869.q: Which sea reptile from Monte San Giorgio is named after Switzerland?
110869.e: Helveticosaurus is named after Helvetia, the Latin name for Switzerland. So far it is known only from Monte San Giorgio.
110869.m: Helveticosaurus has Switzerland in its name.

110870.q: Why is Monte San Giorgio a UNESCO World Heritage site?
110870.e: Very well-preserved fossils of sea reptiles and fish were found on Monte San Giorgio. That is why UNESCO added the mountain to the World Heritage list.
110870.m: Monte San Giorgio is World Heritage because of its fossils.

110871.q: Roughly how old are the famous fossils from Monte San Giorgio?
110871.e: The fossils are about 240 million years old. At that time there was a sea lagoon in this place.
110871.m: The fossils from Monte San Giorgio are about 240 million years old.

110872.q: Which living things made Monte San Giorgio especially well known?
110872.e: On Monte San Giorgio, superbly preserved sea reptiles, fish and invertebrates from a lagoon were found.
110872.m: Monte San Giorgio is famous for sea reptiles and fish.

110873.q: What was special about the reptile Tanystropheus from Monte San Giorgio?
110873.e: Tanystropheus had a neck about as long as its body and tail together. It probably lived on the coast and hunted fish.
110873.m: Tanystropheus was a reptile with a huge neck.

110875.q: Why are the fossils on Monte San Giorgio so well preserved?
a: The oxygen-poor bottom of a lagoon
110875.e: There was hardly any oxygen at the bottom of the lagoon at that time. Dead animals did not rot and were buried in fine mud.
110875.m: Lack of oxygen protected the fossils from decay.

110876.q: What was the predatory land reptile from Monte San Giorgio called, whose name refers to the canton of Ticino?
110876.e: Ticinosuchus means “Ticino crocodile”. It was a relative of the ancestors of crocodiles and lived on land near the lagoon.

110877.q: How do researchers explain that many Plateosaurus were found in one place in Frick?
a: They probably got stuck in the mud
110877.e: A common explanation is that the heavy animals sank into muddy ground and could not get out again. So they were quickly buried.
110877.m: Many Plateosaurus probably got stuck in the mud.

110878.q: Which plant-eating dinosaur was found especially often in the clay pit at Frick?
110878.e: Many skeletons of Plateosaurus were dug up in Frick. The site is one of the most important in Europe for this dinosaur.
110878.m: Many Plateosaurus skeletons were found in Frick.

110879.q: About how many years ago did Plateosaurus live?
110879.e: Plateosaurus lived about 210 million years ago in the Triassic. So it was one of the early dinosaurs.
110879.m: Plateosaurus lived about 210 million years ago.

110880.q: What did Plateosaurus mainly feed on?
110880.e: Plateosaurus had leaf-shaped teeth and a long neck. With these it ate plants, including some way up.

110881.q: About how long could a fully grown Plateosaurus be?
110881.e: Depending on the animal, Plateosaurus reached about 5 to 10 metres in length. It walked on two legs.

110882.q: What raw material is mainly dug out of the clay pit at Frick?
110882.e: Clay for making bricks is dug in the clay pit. Workers and researchers kept coming across dinosaur bones while doing so.
110882.m: Clay is dug in the clay pit at Frick.

110883.q: What kind of dinosaur was newly described from Frick in 2019?
110883.e: The predatory dinosaur Notatesseraeraptor frickensis lived in the Triassic. Its second name refers to the find site, Frick.
110883.m: A predatory dinosaur was also found in Frick.

110884.q: What does the genus name “Plateosaurus” mean?
110884.e: The name comes from Greek: “platys” means broad, “sauros” lizard. You often read the translation “flat lizard”, but “broad lizard” is probably what is meant.

110885.q: Why is Archaeopteryx often called the “first bird”?
a: It had features of birds and reptiles
110885.e: Archaeopteryx had feathers and wings like a bird, but also typical reptile features such as a long bony tail.
110885.m: Archaeopteryx combines features of birds and reptiles.

110886.q: In which country were the fossils of the early bird Archaeopteryx found?
110886.e: Archaeopteryx comes from the fine-grained limestone of the Solnhofen area in Bavaria. This limestone even preserved prints of feathers.

110887.q: In which period did Archaeopteryx live?
110887.e: Archaeopteryx lived about 150 million years ago in the late Jurassic. At that time the Solnhofen area lay by a lagoon.

110888.q: What did Archaeopteryx have on its wings that is usually missing in today's birds?
110888.e: On each wing, Archaeopteryx had three fingers with claws. It could probably use them to hold on.
110888.m: Archaeopteryx had claws on its wings.

110889.q: Which question about Archaeopteryx is still debated among experts today?
110889.e: Its feathers suggest it could fly, but its flight muscles were probably weaker than those of today's birds. Whether it flew actively or rather glided is debated.
110889.m: How well Archaeopteryx flew is still debated.

110890.q: What makes the fossils of Archaeopteryx especially valuable for research?
a: You can even see prints of the feathers in them
They are made of pure gold
They are the oldest fossils on Earth
110890.e: The fine limestone preserved not only the bones but also the feathers as prints. This shows that an animal with reptile features already had feathers.

110891.q: Which animal alive today, with a shell divided into chambers, resembles the ammonites?
110891.e: Like the ammonites, the nautilus has a spiral shell with chambers. It lives in the Indo-Pacific.
110891.m: The nautilus resembles the extinct ammonites.

110892.q: What were the gas-filled chambers in the shell of ammonites for?
110892.e: With gas and liquid in the chambers, ammonites could control how well they floated. In this way they hovered in the water.

110893.q: Which Egyptian god are the ammonites named after?
110893.e: The god Ammon was shown with ram's horns. The spiral shells look like such horns.
110893.m: Ammonites are named after the god Ammon with ram's horns.

110894.q: What does the typically shaped line of the chamber walls on an ammonite help with?
110894.e: The line where the chamber walls meet the shell is called the suture line. It has a typical shape for each species of ammonite.
110894.m: The suture line helps to identify ammonites.

110895.q: Where in Switzerland are ammonites often found?
a: In the limestones of the Jura
In the granite of the Gotthard
In the sand of the Rhine
110895.e: In the Jura and the limestone Alps, sea deposits from the Mesozoic era are widespread. They often contain ammonites.
110895.m: Ammonites are often found in Swiss limestones.

110896.q: Why are many ammonites so good as index fossils?
110896.e: Ammonites quickly developed into new species again and again and lived in seas all over the world. So they often mark short periods of time.
110896.m: Ammonites mark short periods of Earth's history.

110897.q: Where have several well-preserved mammoth bodies with skin and hair been found?
110897.e: In the permanently frozen ground of Siberia, dead bodies are preserved as if in a freezer. Sometimes even skin, fur and stomach contents survive.
110897.m: In the permafrost, mammoths were preserved deep-frozen.

110898.q: Which animal alive today is the closest relative of the woolly mammoth?
110898.e: Comparisons of genetic material show that the mammoth is closest to the Asian elephant.
110898.m: The mammoth is closely related to the Asian elephant.

110899.q: How long ago did the last woolly mammoths live?
110899.e: The last mammoths lived until about 4000 years ago on Wrangel Island in the Arctic Ocean. By then, the pyramids already stood in Egypt.
110899.m: The last mammoths died out about 4000 years ago.

110900.q: Have remains of mammoths also been found in Switzerland?
a: Yes, for example in the canton of Zurich
110900.e: During the Ice Age, mammoths also lived in the Swiss Plateau. Many bones were found in Niederweningen ZH, and a museum displays them.
110900.m: Mammoths once lived in Switzerland too.

110901.q: How was the woolly mammoth adapted to the cold of the Ice Age?
110901.e: Thick fur, a layer of fat and small ears reduced the loss of heat. This let the mammoth survive cold winters.
110901.m: Fur and small ears protected the mammoth from the cold.

110902.q: What are the long, curved teeth of the mammoth called?
110902.e: Mammoth tusks were lengthened front teeth and could grow more than four metres long. The mammoth used them, for example, to push snow aside.

110903.q: What did the woolly mammoth mainly feed on?
110903.e: Mammoths lived on the mammoth steppe and ate mainly grasses, herbs and bushes. Their back teeth were built for grinding.
110903.m: The mammoth ate grasses and herbs.

110904.q: How many great mass extinctions do experts usually distinguish in Earth's history?
110904.e: They are known as the “Big Five”. They include, for example, the extinctions at the end of the Permian and at the end of the Cretaceous.
110904.m: Earth's history has five great mass extinctions.

110905.q: Which mass extinction is considered the biggest in Earth's history?
a: At the end of the Permian
At the end of the Cretaceous
At the end of the Ice Age
At the end of the Jurassic
110905.e: About 252 million years ago, at the end of the Permian, most of all sea species died out. It is estimated at more than 80 per cent.
110905.m: The biggest mass extinction happened at the end of the Permian.

110906.q: What is considered the main cause of the mass extinction at the end of the Permian?
110906.e: Enormous outpourings of lava, the Siberian Traps, released huge amounts of gases. This changed the climate and the seas dramatically.
110906.m: Volcanic activity in Siberia caused the Permian extinction.

110907.q: What is meant by a mass extinction?
a: Many species die out in a short time
110907.e: In a mass extinction, a large part of all species worldwide disappears in what is a short time in Earth's history.
110907.m: In a mass extinction, very many species disappear at once.

110908.q: Why do some researchers today speak of the “sixth mass extinction”?
a: Humans are making many species disappear
110908.e: Because of habitat destruction, overuse and climate change, species are dying out much faster than normal today. That is why people speak of a sixth mass extinction.
110908.m: Humans are causing a new extinction of species.

110909.q: Where did most of the animals live that died in the first great mass extinction about 445 million years ago?
110909.e: At that time almost all animals still lived in the sea. About 445 million years ago, many sea species died out, mainly because of an Ice Age.
110909.m: The first great mass extinction mainly hit sea animals.

110910.q: What often happens after a mass extinction?
a: Surviving groups develop many new species
The Earth turns into a moon
110910.e: Habitats that have become free are taken over by survivors. After the end of the dinosaurs, for example, mammals spread widely.
110910.m: After mass extinctions, many new species arise.

110911.q: Which mass extinction happened about 201 million years ago and cleared the way for the dinosaurs?
a: At the end of the Triassic
At the end of the Permian
At the end of the Cretaceous
At the end of the Cambrian
110911.e: At the end of the Triassic, many rivals of the dinosaurs disappeared. After that, the dinosaurs dominated in the Jurassic and the Cretaceous.
110911.m: After the Triassic extinction, the dinosaurs dominated.

110912.q: Where is the crater of the asteroid that struck about 66 million years ago?
a: On the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico
110912.e: The Chicxulub crater lies mostly under the Yucatán Peninsula and the Gulf of Mexico. Today it is covered by younger rocks.
110912.m: The Chicxulub crater is in Mexico.

110913.q: About how big was the asteroid that struck at the end of the Cretaceous?
110913.e: The asteroid was probably about 10 kilometres across. The crater is more than 150 kilometres wide.
110913.m: An asteroid about 10 kilometres across struck.

110914.q: What probably caused the extinction of the dinosaurs about 66 million years ago?
110914.e: A large asteroid struck in Mexico. Evidence of this was found in a thin layer of rock that contains a substance from space.
110914.m: An asteroid ended the age of the dinosaurs.

110915.q: Which group of dinosaurs survived the impact and lives on today?
110915.e: Only the birds survived as descendants of the dinosaurs. Pterosaurs, by the way, were not dinosaurs and also died out.

110916.q: Why did many plants die after the impact?
110916.e: Dust and soot in the atmosphere blocked out sunlight. Without light there was hardly any photosynthesis, and food chains collapsed.
110916.m: Without sunlight, the food chains collapsed.

110917.q: Besides the asteroid, what is discussed as another cause of the extinction of the dinosaurs?
110917.e: At the same time, giant volcanoes erupted in India and released large amounts of gases. But many experts see the impact as the main cause.
110917.m: Volcanic eruptions also put strain on the climate at the end of the Cretaceous.

110918.q: Which group of animals benefited especially after the extinction of the dinosaurs?
110918.e: Before that, mammals were mostly small. After the large dinosaurs died out, they developed into many new and bigger forms.
110918.m: Mammals spread after the dinosaurs died out.

110919.q: According to what we know today, which huge sea waves did the impact cause?
110919.e: The impact in shallow sea caused giant tsunamis. Traces of them have been found all around the Gulf of Mexico.

110920.q: What can researchers find out from coprolites?
110920.e: Coprolites contain splinters of bone, scales or plant remains. They show what a prehistoric animal fed on.
110920.m: Coprolites reveal the food of prehistoric animals.

110922.q: Which large predatory dinosaur is a giant coprolite found in Saskatchewan, Canada, in 1995 credited to?
110922.e: The find from the late Cretaceous is one of the largest known coprolites of a meat eater. It is credited to a Tyrannosaurus rex.
110922.m: Fossilised droppings of Tyrannosaurus are known too.

110923.q: Which type of fossil do coprolites count as?
110923.e: Coprolites are not body parts but something an animal left behind. That is why they count as trace fossils.

110924.q: How can experts tell that a coprolite comes from a meat eater?
110924.e: Droppings of meat eaters often contain bone splinters and are rich in phosphate. Plant eaters, on the other hand, leave plant remains.
110924.m: Bone remains in a coprolite point to a meat eater.

110925.q: Which tiny living things can also be found in coprolites?
110925.e: Fossilised eggs of gut parasites have been found in some coprolites. They show that prehistoric animals already had parasites.

110926.q: Why are coprolites found much more rarely than bones?
110926.e: Droppings are soft and are quickly broken down by bacteria, insects and the weather. Only under special conditions do they turn to stone.
110926.m: Droppings rarely turn to stone, because they break down quickly.

110927.e: “Ichthys” is Greek for fish, “sauros” for lizard. Ichthyosaurs were reptiles with a fish-like body shape.

110928.e: Ichthyosaurs lived at the time of the dinosaurs, but belonged to a separate group of sea reptiles. Dinosaurs did not live as swimmers in the open sea.
110928.m: Ichthyosaurs were sea reptiles, not dinosaurs.

110929.q: Which animals of today did ichthyosaurs resemble in body shape?
110929.e: Ichthyosaurs had a streamlined body, flippers and a tail fin like dolphins. This similarity came from adapting to the same life in the sea.

110930.q: Which English fossil collector found, with her brother, one of the first known ichthyosaur skeletons in the early 19th century?
110930.e: Mary Anning collected fossils on the coast near Lyme Regis. Around 1811 to 1812, she and her brother Joseph uncovered an ichthyosaur skeleton.
110930.m: Mary Anning found one of the first ichthyosaur skeletons.

110931.q: Which body features show that many ichthyosaurs were good hunters in dark water?
110931.e: Many ichthyosaurs had huge eyes with rings of bone. With them they could spot prey even in deep, dark water.
110931.m: Large eyes helped ichthyosaurs to hunt.

110932.e: Ichthyosaurs have been extinct for millions of years. Their skeletons are found fossilised in rock layers, for example in Holzmaden in Germany or on Monte San Giorgio in Ticino.
110932.m: Ichthyosaurs are known only as fossils.

110933.q: What did ichthyosaurs mainly feed on?
110933.e: Stomach contents show that ichthyosaurs ate fish and cephalopods. Their long snouts had many sharp teeth.

110934.q: Which organ did ichthyosaurs have to use to breathe?
110934.e: As reptiles, ichthyosaurs breathed with lungs. So they had to come up to the surface of the water for air.
110934.m: Ichthyosaurs breathed with lungs, like dolphins.

110935.q: Into which three periods is the Mesozoic era divided?
110935.e: The Mesozoic lasted from about 252 to 66 million years ago. It is the age of the dinosaurs.
110935.m: The Mesozoic consists of the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous.

110936.q: Which mountain range is the “Jurassic” period named after?
110936.e: The rocks of the Jura Mountains on the border between Switzerland and France gave the period its name. Alexander von Humboldt coined the term.
110936.m: The Jurassic period is named after the Jura Mountains.

110937.q: What is the era of Earth's history we live in today called?
110937.e: The Cenozoic began about 66 million years ago, after the dinosaurs died out.

110938.q: In which period did large coal deposits form from huge swamp forests?
110938.e: The name Carboniferous comes from the Latin “carbo” for coal. Coal formed from dead plants of the swamp forests.
110938.m: Much coal formed in the Carboniferous.

110939.q: What does the name of the “Triassic” period refer to?
110939.e: In Germany, the Triassic is divided into three layers of rock: red sandstone, shell limestone and Keuper. This division into three gave the period its name.
110939.m: The Triassic is named after a division of rock layers into three.

110940.q: Which period of the Cenozoic, with several Ice Ages, is still going on today?
110940.e: The Quaternary began about 2.6 million years ago. It is marked by changes between cold periods and warm periods.
110940.m: We live in the Quaternary, the age of Ice Ages.

110941.q: Which rock is the Cretaceous period named after?
110941.e: At this time, thick layers of chalk were laid down, for example the White Cliffs of Dover or the cliffs of Rügen.
110941.m: The Cretaceous is named after the white limestone rock chalk.

110942.q: Which dinosaurs is Plateosaurus an early relative of?
110942.e: Plateosaurus belongs to the sauropodomorphs. Later, giant long-necked dinosaurs such as Brachiosaurus came from this group.
110942.m: Plateosaurus is an early relative of the long-necked dinosaurs.

110943.q: What happens when wood turns to stone?
110943.e: Water with dissolved silica gets into the wood. Quartz gradually replaces the wood material, and often even the tree rings remain visible.
110943.m: In petrified wood, quartz has replaced the wood.

110944.q: The Precambrian is the oldest part of Earth's history. Roughly how much of all Earth's history does it cover?
110944.e: The Precambrian stretches from the formation of the Earth to about 540 million years ago. That is about 88 per cent of Earth's history.
110944.m: The Precambrian is the longest part of Earth's history.

110945.q: Which part of the human brain is the biggest?
110945.e: The cerebrum makes up by far the biggest part of the human brain and covers the other parts of the brain almost completely.
110945.m: The cerebrum is the biggest part of our brain.

110946.q: What is the outer, heavily folded layer of the cerebrum called?
110946.e: The cerebral cortex is only a few millimetres thick and lies on the outside of the cerebrum.
110946.m: The cerebral cortex forms the outer layer of the cerebrum.

110947.q: Why is the cerebral cortex folded into many ridges and grooves?
a: So that more surface fits inside the skull
So that the brain is lighter
So that knocks are cushioned better
110947.e: Thanks to the folds, a large cortex surface with many nerve cells fits into the limited space of the skull.
110947.m: The folds increase the surface of the cerebral cortex.

110948.q: Which lobe of the cerebrum lies directly behind the forehead?
110948.e: The frontal lobe is the front lobe of the brain and is important for planning, acting and movement.
110948.m: The frontal lobe is at the front, behind the forehead.

110949.q: What does the grey matter of the cerebral cortex mainly consist of?
110949.e: The cell bodies of the nerve cells lie in the grey matter. The white matter underneath consists mainly of nerve fibres with pale myelin sheaths.
110949.m: Grey matter mainly contains the cell bodies of nerve cells.

110950.q: In which lobe of the cerebrum is the auditory cortex?
110950.e: The auditory cortex lies in the temporal lobe, at the side of the head, roughly level with the ears.
110950.m: Hearing is processed in the temporal lobe.

110951.q: In which lobe of the cerebrum are touch sensations from the skin mainly processed?
110951.e: Behind the central groove, in the parietal lobe, lies the somatosensory cortex, which processes touch, pressure and temperature.
110951.m: Touch sensations are processed in the parietal lobe.

110952.q: What job does the motor cortex of the cerebrum do?
110952.e: The motor cortex lies in front of the central groove in the frontal lobe and sends commands for conscious movements to the muscles.
110952.m: The motor cortex starts our conscious movements.

110953.q: Which abilities are mainly linked to the cerebrum?
110953.e: Conscious perception, thinking, language, learning and memory arise in the cerebrum.
110953.m: We think, learn and remember with the cerebrum.

a: At the back of the head below the cerebrum
110954.e: The cerebellum lies in the lower back part of the skull, below the cerebrum and behind the brainstem.
110954.m: The cerebellum sits at the back of the head below the cerebrum.

110955.q: What is the most important job of the cerebellum?
110955.e: The cerebellum makes sure that movements are finely tuned, smooth and balanced.
110955.m: The cerebellum coordinates movements and keeps us balanced.

110956.q: Which test does a doctor use to check whether the cerebellum is working well?
a: Bringing your finger to your nose with your eyes closed
110956.e: For the finger-to-nose test, movements must be precisely coordinated. If the cerebellum is not working properly, you miss your nose or shake.
110956.m: The finger-to-nose test checks the cerebellum.

110957.q: Which skill becomes automatic after lots of practice because the cerebellum has stored the sequence of movements?
110957.e: The cerebellum helps us learn sequences of movements. Practised movements like riding a bike then happen without thinking.
110957.m: The cerebellum helps store practised movements like riding a bike.

110958.q: Which part of the brain is especially busy when you balance on one leg?
110958.e: The cerebellum processes messages from the organ of balance and the muscles. With small corrections it makes sure you do not fall over.
110958.m: The cerebellum works when you balance.

110959.q: Which part of the brain, although it is small, contains most of the brain's nerve cells?
110959.e: The cerebellum contains a huge number of tiny granule cells. That is why it holds well over half of all the nerve cells in the brain.
110959.m: The cerebellum is small but contains the most nerve cells.

110960.q: What is a typical result of damage to the cerebellum?
a: Loss of the sense of smell
110960.e: If the cerebellum is damaged, movements become inaccurate and shaky, and balance is disturbed. This is called ataxia.
110960.m: A damaged cerebellum makes movements unsteady.

110961.q: How many halves does the cerebellum have?
110961.e: The cerebellum has a left and a right half. Between them is a narrow middle part called the vermis.

110962.q: Which vital processes are controlled by the brainstem?
110962.e: The brainstem contains centres that automatically control breathing, heartbeat and blood pressure.
110962.m: The brainstem keeps breathing and the heartbeat going.

110963.q: Which of the following parts belongs to the brainstem?
110963.e: The brainstem includes the midbrain, the pons and the medulla oblongata.
110963.m: The medulla oblongata is part of the brainstem.

110964.q: Which part of the brain leads directly into the spinal cord?
110964.e: The medulla oblongata is the lowest part of the brainstem and leads into the spinal cord at the opening at the base of the skull.
110964.m: The spinal cord begins at the medulla oblongata.

110965.q: What is the bulging part of the brainstem called, through which the cerebrum is connected with the cerebellum?
110965.e: The pons bulges out at the front of the brainstem. Signals from the cerebrum to the cerebellum travel along its nerve pathways.
110965.m: The pons connects the cerebrum with the cerebellum.

110966.q: In which part of the brain are protective reflexes such as coughing, sneezing and swallowing controlled?
110966.e: The centres for coughing, sneezing, swallowing and being sick lie in the medulla oblongata of the brainstem.
110966.m: Coughing and swallowing are controlled in the medulla oblongata.

a: Between the cerebrum and the spinal cord
Low down in the back near the pelvis
Behind the eyes in the nose
110967.e: The brainstem forms the lowest part of the brain. It connects the cerebrum with the spinal cord.
110967.m: The brainstem connects the brain and the spinal cord.

110968.q: Which part of the brain is, among other things, important for whether we are awake or asleep?
110968.e: The brainstem contains a net-like network of nerve cells. Among other things, it controls how awake and alert we are.
110968.m: The brainstem helps to control waking and sleep.

110969.q: What is the thick bundle of fibres connecting the two halves of the cerebrum called?
110969.e: The corpus callosum consists of many millions of nerve fibres and connects the left half of the brain with the right.
110969.m: The corpus callosum connects the two halves of the brain.

110970.q: What is affected in aphasia after a stroke?
110970.e: In aphasia, the language centres in the brain are damaged. People affected have trouble finding words or do not understand what is said.
110970.m: Aphasia is a language disorder caused by brain damage.

110971.q: In which half of the brain are the language centres in most right-handed people?
110971.e: In over 90 percent of right-handed people, the main language centres are in the left half of the brain.
110971.m: In most people, language is processed on the left side of the brain.

110972.q: Which side of the body is often paralysed when a stroke affects the left half of the brain?
a: Only the left side of the face
110972.e: Because the nerve pathways cross over, damage in the left half of the brain leads to paralysis on the right side of the body.
110972.m: A stroke on the left often paralyses the right side of the body.

110973.q: What divides the cerebrum into a left and a right half?
110973.e: A deep groove runs from front to back and separates the two halves of the cerebrum. Lower down they are connected by the corpus callosum.
110973.m: A deep groove separates the two halves of the cerebrum.

110974.q: Which half of the brain controls the movements of the left hand?
110974.e: The nerve pathways cross over on their way to the body. That is why the right half of the brain controls the left side of the body and the other way round.
110974.m: The right half of the brain controls the left side of the body.

110975.q: Why can speech therapy help after a stroke?
a: The brain can form new connections
110975.e: With lots of practice, other parts of the brain can partly take over tasks. That way many people affected learn to speak better again.
110975.m: The brain can form new connections through practice.

110976.q: Do the two halves of the brain work in exactly the same way?
a: No, they partly have different jobs
Yes, they do exactly the same
No, one half is always asleep
110976.e: The two halves of the brain share out some tasks. For example, the language centres are usually in the left half.
110976.m: The two halves of the brain partly have different jobs.

110978.q: Why do we not normally notice the blind spot in our own eye in everyday life?
a: The brain fills in the gap in the picture
The blind spot is too small for light
110978.e: Where the optic nerve leaves the eye there are no sensory cells. The visual system fills in the gap with the surroundings and with the images from the other eye.
110978.m: The brain fills in gaps in the picture that the eye does not provide.

110979.q: What happens in the visual cortex?
a: Signals from the eyes are processed into pictures
110979.e: The eye turns light into electrical signals. Only the visual cortex processes these signals into what we consciously see.
110979.m: The visual cortex turns nerve signals into pictures.

110980.q: Why do we see the world the right way up, even though the image on the retina is upside down?
a: The brain interprets the image correctly
The pupil turns the image round
The tear fluid mirrors the image
110980.e: The lens creates an upside-down image on the retina. Our visual system has learned to interpret this image so that we see up and down correctly.
110980.m: The brain interprets the upside-down retinal image correctly.

110981.q: Which visual cortex processes what lies in the left visual field?
a: The visual cortex of the right hemisphere
The visual cortex of the left hemisphere
The cortex of the frontal lobe
110981.e: Because the visual pathway partly crosses over, information from the left visual field of both eyes reaches the right visual cortex.
110981.m: The left visual field is processed in the right visual cortex.

110982.q: How do the signals from the eyes reach the visual cortex?
a: Through the optic nerve and visual pathway
110982.e: The retina turns light into nerve signals. These travel along the optic nerve and the visual pathway to the visual cortex at the back of the head.
110982.m: Visual signals travel along the optic nerve and visual pathway to the visual cortex.

110983.q: Why do you sometimes “see stars” after a hard blow to the back of the head?
a: Because the visual cortex there is stimulated
Because the eyes briefly fall out
Because the ears then hear light
110983.e: The visual cortex is at the back of the head. If it is stimulated by a blow, flashes of light appear even though no light is entering the eye.
110983.m: The visual cortex at the back of the head turns signals into pictures.

110984.q: What can damage to both visual cortices cause, even though the eyes are healthy?
110984.e: Without the visual cortex, the signals from the eyes cannot be processed into pictures. This is called cortical blindness.
110984.m: Without a working visual cortex you are blind, despite healthy eyes.

110985.q: What do many nerve cells in the visual cortex react to especially strongly?
110985.e: Researchers found that cells in the visual cortex react to particular shapes such as edges and lines. From these the brain puts together whole pictures.
110985.m: The visual cortex builds pictures out of edges and lines.

110986.q: What runs through the spinal canal below the end of the spinal cord?
110986.e: Below the spinal cord, only nerve roots continue downwards. Because the bundle looks like a horse's tail, it is called the cauda equina, Latin for horse's tail.
110986.m: Below the spinal cord, only nerve fibres continue.

110987.q: Roughly how long is the spinal cord of an adult?
110987.e: The spinal cord of an adult is about 40 to 50 centimetres long and about as thick as a little finger.
110987.m: The spinal cord is about 45 centimetres long.

110988.q: Where does the spinal cord end in adults?
a: In the lower back, above the pelvis
Right at the bottom in the tailbone
110988.e: The spine grows longer than the spinal cord. That is why the cord ends in the upper lumbar region, and below that only nerve fibres continue.
110988.m: The spinal cord ends in the upper lumbar region.

110989.q: What shape is the grey matter in a cross-section of the spinal cord?
110989.e: In cross-section, the grey matter lies on the inside and looks like a butterfly or an H. The white matter lies around it.
110989.m: The grey matter in the spinal cord looks like a butterfly.

110991.q: Why is cerebrospinal fluid taken with a needle in the lower back?
a: There is no spinal cord there any more
110991.e: The spinal cord ends higher up. If the needle goes in between two lumbar vertebrae, the risk of injuring it is very low.
110991.m: Cerebrospinal fluid is taken in the lower back because the spinal cord no longer runs there.

110992.q: Which fluid surrounds the brain and spinal cord and protects them from knocks?
110992.e: Cerebrospinal fluid bathes the brain and spinal cord like a water cushion and absorbs shocks.
110992.m: Cerebrospinal fluid cushions the brain and spinal cord.

110993.q: What branches off between the vertebrae to the left and right of the spinal cord?
a: Nerves that lead into the body
110993.e: Nerves come out in pairs between the vertebrae. They connect the spinal cord with skin, muscles and organs. Humans have 31 such pairs.
110993.m: Pairs of nerves run from the spinal cord to the whole body.

110994.q: In the knee-jerk reflex, what happens when the doctor taps below the kneecap with the little hammer?
110994.e: The tap briefly stretches the thigh muscle. It contracts as a reflex and straightens the lower leg.
110994.m: In the knee-jerk reflex, the lower leg kicks forwards.

110995.q: Why do many reflexes happen especially quickly?
a: Because they are switched in the spinal cord
Because the muscles are especially big
