111552.e: It flowers from about July to October. Then whole embankments and areas of waste ground glow yellow.
111552.m: Goldenrod flowers in late summer and autumn.

111553.q: How does Canadian goldenrod form such dense patches?
a: with buds in the flowers that grow into new plants
111553.e: Through underground runners called rhizomes, one plant keeps forming new shoots. This creates dense patches where other plants can hardly find room.
111553.m: With its rhizomes, goldenrod takes over whole areas.

111554.q: Which valuable habitats does Canadian goldenrod especially threaten in Switzerland?
a: Rock faces in the high mountains
111554.e: Many rare plants live in fen meadows and poor grassland. Goldenrod can grow over them and push them out.
111554.m: Goldenrods threaten meadows that are rich in species.

111555.q: How are larger patches of Canadian goldenrod fought?
a: by mowing several times a year before it flowers
by mowing once after the seeds are ripe
111555.e: Mowing again and again before flowering weakens the rhizomes and stops seeds from forming. Smaller patches can also be pulled up.
111555.m: Goldenrods are mown several times before they flower.

111556.q: Which other invasive goldenrod from North America is widespread in Switzerland?
111556.e: Giant goldenrod, which flowers later, also comes from North America and is invasive. European goldenrod, on the other hand, is native here.
111556.m: Besides Canadian goldenrod, giant goldenrod is also invasive.

111557.q: Why was Canadian goldenrod also valued by beekeepers in the past?
a: It provides lots of nectar and pollen late in the year.
It drives wasps away from the beehive.
111557.e: When many other plants have finished flowering, it still provides food for bees. That is why it used to be planted as bee forage.
111557.m: Goldenrod used to be popular as late food for bees.

111558.q: Which country does the butterfly bush originally come from?
111558.e: The butterfly bush is native to China. It came to Europe as an ornamental shrub.
111558.m: The butterfly bush originally comes from China.

111559.q: Why is the butterfly bush (Buddleja) called that?
a: Its flowers attract lots of butterflies.
It only flowers when butterflies are flying.
111559.e: The scented flowers offer plenty of nectar. That is why lots of butterflies often sit on them in summer.
111559.m: Butterflies love the nectar of the butterfly bush.

111560.q: Why does the butterfly bush still do little to help native butterflies?
a: Their caterpillars can hardly eat its leaves.
Its nectar is poisonous to butterflies.
111560.e: The adult butterflies do drink its nectar. But the caterpillars of most native species find no food on it.
111560.m: The butterfly bush is not a food plant for caterpillars.

111561.q: Where does the butterfly bush often grow wild?
a: on railway land and gravel areas
111561.e: It loves warm, open and stony places. That is why you find it on railway land, in gravel pits and on gravel banks of rivers.
111561.m: The butterfly bush likes to settle on stony ground.

111562.q: What should you do if there is still a butterfly bush in your garden?
a: cut off the faded flower heads before the seeds ripen
collect the seeds and give them away
dump the branches in the forest
111562.e: The seeds ripen in the faded flower spikes and are spread by the wind. If you cut the spikes off in time, you stop it spreading.

111563.q: Is the butterfly bush closely related to the real lilac?
a: No, despite its name it is not
Yes, it is a kind of lilac
Yes, it is the wild lilac
111563.e: The butterfly bush's scientific name is Buddleja davidii. It is not closely related to the real lilac of the genus Syringa, though its flowers look similar. In German it is called “summer lilac”.
111563.m: The butterfly bush is not a real lilac.

111564.q: How many seeds can a single butterfly bush produce in a year?
111564.e: One bush produces up to about 3 million tiny seeds. They can stay able to sprout in the soil for a long time.
111564.m: A single butterfly bush can produce millions of seeds.

111565.q: Which flower colour is most common in the butterfly bush?
111565.e: The long, cone-shaped flower heads are usually violet to lilac. Garden varieties also come in white or pink.
111565.m: The butterfly bush usually has purple flowers.

111566.q: Why is ragweed (Ambrosia) dangerous for many people?
111566.e: Ragweed pollen is one of the strongest triggers of allergies. It can cause hay fever and asthma.
111566.m: Ragweed pollen is a strong allergy trigger.

111567.q: Which continent does ragweed come from?
111567.e: Ragweed comes from North America. It spread in Europe mainly during the 20th century.

111568.q: How was ragweed often brought into gardens?
111568.e: Ragweed seeds were often found in seed mixes for birds. They then sprouted underneath bird feeders.
111568.m: Ragweed often came into gardens with bird food.

111569.q: What is the rule for ragweed in Switzerland?
a: It must be reported and removed.
It may be sold as an ornamental plant.
It is grown as a medicinal plant.
111569.e: Anyone who finds ragweed must remove it and report the find. This is meant to stop it spreading in Switzerland.
111569.m: In Switzerland, ragweed must be reported and removed.

111570.q: In which season does ragweed pollen fly?
111570.e: It flowers from about August to October. This makes the pollen season last into autumn for people with allergies.
111570.m: Ragweed makes the pollen season last into autumn.

111571.q: Where does ragweed often grow in our area?
a: On roadsides, building sites and under bird feeders
111571.e: Ragweed likes open, disturbed ground. Under bird feeders it grows from seeds that were in the bird food.
111571.m: Ragweed grows on open ground and under bird feeders.

111572.q: What should you wear when pulling up ragweed?
a: Gloves, and a dust mask when it is flowering
111572.e: The plant sap can irritate the skin. When the plants are flowering, a mask protects you from the allergy-causing pollen.
111572.m: Only pull up ragweed while wearing gloves.

111573.e: Ragweed is pollinated by the wind and produces huge amounts of light pollen grains. These can be carried far through the air.
111573.m: Ragweed pollen is spread by the wind.

111574.q: What makes ragweed pollen especially troublesome?
a: Even very few pollen grains cause symptoms.
It is so big that you can see it.
111574.e: Just a few pollen grains per cubic metre of air can cause symptoms in sensitive people. Other pollen only has an effect in larger amounts.
111574.m: Even tiny amounts of ragweed pollen can trigger allergies.

111575.q: How does cherry laurel get from gardens into forests?
a: Birds eat the fruits and spread the seeds.
The wind carries its leaves away.
Deer carry branches into the forest.
111575.e: Blackbirds and other birds eat the black fruits. Later they drop the seeds somewhere else in their droppings.
111575.m: Birds spread cherry laurel into forests.

111576.q: Which parts of the cherry laurel are especially poisonous?
111576.e: The leaves and seeds contain substances that can turn into poisonous hydrogen cyanide. The fruit flesh is less poisonous, but should not be eaten either.
111576.m: The leaves and seeds of cherry laurel are poisonous.

111577.q: Why is cherry laurel so popular as a hedge plant?
a: It is evergreen and you cannot see through it.
It keeps its flowers in winter.
111577.e: Its leathery leaves stay green all year round. So it gives privacy even in winter.
111577.m: Cherry laurel stays green all year round.

111578.q: Which region does cherry laurel come from?
111578.e: It is native from the Balkans through Asia Minor to the Caucasus. From there it came to Central Europe as an ornamental plant.
111578.m: Cherry laurel comes from south-eastern Europe and western Asia.

111579.q: Why is cherry laurel of little value for native insects?
a: Only a few insects can use it as food.
It kills all insects with scents.
111579.e: Native insects are adapted to native plants. Only a few of them find food on cherry laurel.
111579.m: A cherry laurel hedge offers native insects little food.

111580.q: Since 2024, cherry laurel may no longer be sold in Switzerland. What is the rule for hedges that were planted before?
a: They must be cut down at once
They must be registered with the federal government
They may no longer be trimmed
111580.e: The ban covers selling, giving away and importing. Plants that are already in gardens are not affected.
111580.m: Existing cherry laurel hedges do not have to be removed.

111581.q: Which plant is a native alternative to a cherry laurel hedge?
111581.e: Hornbeam is native to Switzerland and can easily be trimmed into a thick hedge. Its dry leaves often stay on until spring.
111581.m: Native hedge plants are valuable for nature.

111582.q: Which plant is cherry laurel closely related to?
111582.e: Like the sweet cherry, cherry laurel belongs to the genus Prunus. It is not related to the bay laurel, whose leaves are used as a herb.
111582.m: Cherry laurel is a relative of the cherry.

111583.q: Which country does the tree of heaven come from?
111583.e: The tree of heaven is native to China. It was brought to Europe in the 18th century.
111583.m: The tree of heaven originally comes from China.

111584.q: Apart from seeds, how does the tree of heaven reproduce?
111584.e: New shoots keep growing from its roots. This creates dense groups of young trees.
111584.m: The tree of heaven grows new trees from its roots.

111585.q: What often happens if you simply cut down a tree of heaven?
a: It sprouts strongly again from the stump and roots.
It turns into a shrub without leaves.
111585.e: After it is cut down, it forms lots of new shoots. That is why special methods are needed to control it.
111585.m: Simply cutting down a tree of heaven encourages new shoots.

111586.q: For which kind of animal farming was the tree of heaven also planted in Europe in the 19th century?
111586.e: Its leaves were food for the ailanthus silkmoth. People wanted to make silk with this caterpillar.
111586.m: The tree of heaven was once food for silkworms.

111587.q: How does the tree of heaven hold back the growth of other plants?
a: It releases inhibiting substances into the soil.
It shades them only at night.
111587.e: Its roots and leaves contain substances that stop other plants from sprouting and growing. This effect is called allelopathy.
111587.m: The tree of heaven fights its neighbours with chemicals.

111588.q: What do you notice when you crush the leaves of a tree of heaven?
111588.e: Crushed leaves give off an unpleasant smell. The male flowers also smell strong.
111588.m: Tree of heaven leaves smell unpleasant when crushed.

111589.q: Why does the tree of heaven cope well in cities?
a: It can stand heat, drought and poor soil.
It only grows in clean mountain air.
It needs fresh spring water every day.
111589.e: It even grows in cracks in walls, on railway land and on wasteland. There it has little competition.
111589.m: The tree of heaven is a tough city dweller.

111590.q: What do the fruits of the tree of heaven look like?
111590.e: The seeds sit in long, twisted wings. This lets the wind carry them away.
111590.m: The tree of heaven has winged fruits.

111591.q: What is the rule for the tree of heaven in Switzerland today?
a: It may no longer be planted.
It has been declared the national tree.
It must stand in every park.
111591.e: The tree of heaven is listed in Annex 2.1 of the Release Ordinance. It may no longer be sold, planted or propagated; the only thing allowed is to control it.
111591.m: In Switzerland you may no longer plant the tree of heaven.

111592.q: Which continent does annual fleabane come from?
111592.e: Annual fleabane is native to North America. In Europe it was first grown as an ornamental plant.
111592.m: Annual fleabane comes from North America.

111593.q: Which native flower is annual fleabane often confused with because of its flowers?
111593.e: It has white ray petals around a yellow centre, like the ox-eye daisy. But its flower heads are much smaller.
111593.m: Annual fleabane looks like a small ox-eye daisy.

111594.q: What is special about the way annual fleabane makes seeds?
a: The seeds form even without pollination.
It needs two plants to do it.
It only makes seeds every ten years.
The seeds grow in the roots.
111594.e: It can make seeds without fertilisation. That is why even a single plant produces lots of seeds that can sprout.
111594.m: Annual fleabane needs no pollinators for its seeds.

111595.q: Despite its name, what is true about how long annual fleabane lives?
a: It can also live for two years.
It always lives only a few weeks.
It always lives exactly one month.
It lives for several hundred years.
111595.e: It often survives the winter as a rosette of leaves and only flowers in the second year. So it lives for one or two years.
111595.m: Annual fleabane often lives longer than a year.

111596.q: What is the most effective way to get rid of annual fleabane?
a: pull it up with its roots before it flowers
111596.e: Its roots are shallow, so it is easy to pull up. If you remove it with its roots before it flowers, it can neither grow back nor make seeds.
111596.m: Pull up fleabane by the roots before it flowers.

111597.q: Why does mowing alone do little against annual fleabane?
a: It sprouts again and flowers once more.
111597.e: After cutting, it grows new stems from its base and soon flowers again, often lower down. So it still makes seeds.

111598.q: In which habitats does annual fleabane spread especially well?
a: in meadows, on roadsides and wasteland
111598.e: It loves open, sunny areas. That is why you find it in meadows, on roadsides, on embankments and on wasteland.
111598.m: Annual fleabane likes sunny, open places.

111599.q: Where does the German name “Berufkraut” for fleabane probably come from?
a: from the belief that it protects against being bewitched
from its use in vocational schools
111599.e: In the past, the German word “berufen” meant something like “to bewitch”. People believed that plants of this genus protected against spells.
111599.m: The German name Berufkraut comes from old folk beliefs.

111600.q: What do you call plants from distant countries that spread strongly here and cause damage?
111600.e: Neophytes are plants that people have brought in from elsewhere. They are called invasive when they spread strongly and push out native species.
111600.m: Invasive neophytes spread strongly and push out native plants.

111601.q: What does the Swiss Release Ordinance regulate?
a: how organisms are handled in the environment
the opening hours of garden centres
111601.e: Its full title is “Ordinance on the Handling of Organisms in the Environment”. This also covers invasive non-native plants.
111601.m: The Release Ordinance regulates how organisms are handled in the environment.

111602.q: What are you allowed to do with banned invasive plants such as Himalayan balsam?
a: Grow more of them in the garden
111602.e: Any handling of banned invasive plants is forbidden, such as selling, giving away and planting. The only thing allowed is getting rid of them.
111602.m: With banned invasive species, only getting rid of them is allowed.

111603.q: Which palm may no longer be sold in Switzerland because it grows wild in the forests of southern Switzerland?
111603.e: The Chinese windmill palm is often called the Ticino palm and is spreading in the forests of Ticino. That is why it may no longer be passed on to others or imported.
111603.m: The Ticino palm is really an invasive windmill palm from Asia.

111604.q: Who in Switzerland is mainly responsible for enforcing the bans on invasive plants?
111604.e: The federal government makes the rules and the cantons put them into practice. Only import controls are the federal government's job.
111604.m: The cantons make sure the bans on neophytes are followed.

111605.q: Why are invasive plants a problem for nature?
a: They turn the soil into sand
111605.e: Invasive plants often grow fast and thick. They take light and space from native plants, and animals lose their food too.
111605.m: Invasive plants push out native species.

111606.q: Where should invasive plants go once they have been pulled up?
a: In the household rubbish, not on the compost
At the edge of the forest
111606.e: On the compost or out in nature, seeds and pieces of root can keep growing. Household rubbish is burnt, so they can no longer spread.
111606.m: Invasive plants go in the household rubbish.

111607.q: Why do customs officers check whether banned plants are being brought into Switzerland?
a: So that no more invasive species enter the country
So that garden centres sell more
So that there are more bees
111607.e: Many invasive plants come into the country through trade. Checks at the border are meant to stop new problem plants being brought in.
111607.m: Customs helps keep invasive plants out.

a: A plant brought in from elsewhere that spreads strongly and causes harm
A native plant that is threatened with extinction
A plant that only grows high in the mountains
A new vegetable variety from the garden centre
111608.e: Neophytes are plants that were brought to us from other parts of the world. They are called invasive when they spread strongly and push out native plants or cause other damage.
111608.m: Invasive neophytes are introduced plants that spread and cause harm.

111609.q: Which plants were on the Black List?
111609.e: The Black List contained invasive neophytes whose damage had been proven. Their spread was to be stopped.
111609.m: The Black List contained harmful invasive neophytes.

111610.q: Why should you not plant invasive neophytes such as the butterfly bush in your garden?
111610.e: Invasive neophytes spread from gardens into nature. There they take space and light from native plants.
111610.m: Invasive neophytes push out native plants.

111611.q: What kinds of damage were considered when adding a plant to the Black List?
a: to biodiversity, health or the economy
111611.e: A species went on the list if it harmed nature, people or the economy. This includes things like allergies or damage to riverbanks.
111611.m: The Black List considers damage to nature, health and the economy.

111612.q: Which of these plants was on Switzerland's Black List?
111612.e: Giant hogweed comes from the Caucasus and is invasive. The much smaller common hogweed, on the other hand, is native.
111612.m: Giant hogweed is an invasive neophyte.

111613.q: How do you correctly dispose of invasive neophytes pulled up in the garden?
a: In the household rubbish, not on the compost
On the compost heap in the garden
In the stream behind the house
111613.e: On the compost, seeds and pieces of root can survive and keep spreading. That is why invasive neophytes belong in the household rubbish, which is burnt.
111613.m: Invasive neophytes belong in the household rubbish, not on the compost.

111614.q: What is the counterpart to the Black List called, which lists threatened native species?
111614.e: The Red List shows which species are threatened or close to extinction. The Black List, on the other hand, names harmful non-native species.
111614.m: The Red List names threatened species.

111615.q: Why should flowering neophytes not go on the garden compost?
a: Their seeds can survive and spread.
They make the compost too acidic.
111615.e: Garden compost often does not get hot enough to kill all the seeds. They would then be spread again with the compost.
111615.m: Seeds of neophytes belong in the household rubbish.

111616.q: Why is it worth tackling neophytes early?
a: Small patches can still be removed completely.
Large patches disappear on their own.
111616.e: As long as there are only a few plants, getting rid of them is easy and cheap. Removing large patches takes many years and costs a lot.
111616.m: The earlier you tackle neophytes, the easier it is.

111617.q: Why must you protect your skin when tackling giant hogweed?
a: Its sap causes burns in sunlight.
It turns your skin green for ever.
111617.e: The sap contains substances that make the skin sensitive to light. In sunlight, painful blisters appear, like a burn.
111617.m: Only touch giant hogweed while wearing protective clothing.

111618.q: Why must areas be checked for several years after neophytes have been removed?
a: Seeds in the soil can still sprout years later.
The law requires mowing every day.
111618.e: The soil often holds a store of seeds that can still sprout, called the seed bank. New plants grow from it even years later.
111618.m: With neophytes you need patience and follow-up checks.

111619.q: What can you do in your own garden to stop neophytes spreading?
a: scatter seeds of exotic plants in the forest
throw garden waste into the stream
111619.e: Native plants do not spread invasively and provide food for many animals. This makes a nature-friendly garden.
111619.m: Native garden plants are good for nature.

111620.q: Why are herbicides rarely used to control neophytes?
a: They also harm other plants and waters.
They only work on native plants.
111620.e: Weedkillers also hit plants you want to keep and can get into the water. That is why they are only used in exceptional cases and by experts.
111620.m: With neophytes, pulling up and mowing come before poison.

111621.q: What is the best way to remove young seedlings of invasive trees and shrubs?
a: pull them up with their roots
111621.e: Small seedlings can still easily be pulled out of the ground with their roots. Later the roots hold firm and sprout again after being cut.
111621.m: It is best to pull up young woody plants with their roots.

111622.q: What happens to a tree if you remove a ring of bark all the way round it?
111622.e: Sap carrying nutrients flows under the bark. If the bark is removed all the way round, this flow of sap is cut off and the tree slowly dies. This is one way to control invasive trees, for example.
111622.m: Without a ring of bark all round, a tree slowly dies.

111623.q: Why is a classic weather station hut painted white?
a: White is easier to see in the snow.
White protects the wood from fungi.
111623.e: A white surface reflects the sun's rays. So the hut does not heat up and the thermometer measures the real air temperature.
111623.m: The white paint stops the weather hut from heating up.

111624.q: Why do weather huts have side walls made of slanted slats?
a: Air can flow through, but the sun cannot get in.
So birds can nest in them.
So you can hear the wind.
111624.e: Fresh outside air flows through the slats to the instruments. At the same time, they protect against direct sun and rain.
111624.m: Slats let air in and keep sun and rain out.

111626.q: Why is wind measured high above the ground at a weather station?
a: Because obstacles on the ground slow the wind down
Because the wind is warmer up there
Because you can see better there
Because otherwise animals eat the instrument
111626.e: Houses, trees and bushes slow the wind near the ground. That is why it is usually measured at a height of 10 metres, where it is less disturbed.
111626.m: Wind is measured high above the ground.

111627.q: What kind of ground should a weather station ideally stand on?
a: on short-cut grass in an open spot
right next to a house wall
111627.e: Grass heats up less than tarmac, and without buildings or trees nearby, temperature and wind are not distorted. That way, measurements from different stations can be compared.
111627.m: A weather station needs an open site over grass.

111628.q: How often do MeteoSwiss's automatic stations send their measurements?
111628.e: The automatic stations send their data every 10 minutes. This means even quick changes in the weather can be followed.
111628.m: Automatic weather stations measure every 10 minutes.

111629.q: Which instrument measures hours of sunshine with a glass ball that burns a trace into a paper strip?
111629.e: The glass ball focuses sunlight like a magnifying glass. The burn mark on the paper shows how long the sun has been shining.
111629.m: A sunshine recorder measures how long the sun shines.

111630.q: What does a wind gauge, also called an anemometer, measure?
111630.e: An anemometer often has small cups that spin in the wind. The faster they spin, the stronger the wind is blowing.
111630.m: An anemometer measures how fast the wind blows.

111631.q: What is the average air pressure at sea level?
111631.e: Standard air pressure at sea level is 1013.25 hectopascals. This value is used as an international reference.
111631.m: At sea level, normal air pressure is about 1013 hectopascals.

111632.q: Which older unit is exactly equal to one hectopascal?
111632.e: One hectopascal and one millibar are exactly the same size. Air pressure used to be given in millibars.
111632.m: One hectopascal is exactly one millibar.

111633.e: “Hecto” means a hundred. So 1013 times 100 gives 101,300 pascals.
111633.m: One hectopascal is a hundred pascals.

111634.q: At roughly what height is air pressure only half as high as at sea level?
111634.e: Air pressure keeps falling with height. At about 5.5 kilometres up, only half of the air's mass is above us.
111634.m: At about 5.5 kilometres up, air pressure is only half as high.

111635.q: Near the ground, air pressure drops by about 1 hPa for every 8 metres of height. By roughly how much does it drop if you climb 80 metres higher?
111635.e: 80 metres divided by 8 metres gives 10. So the air pressure drops by about 10 hectopascals.
111635.m: The higher you climb, the lower the air pressure.

111636.q: In which direction does air basically flow?
a: from high to low air pressure
from low to high air pressure
111636.e: Air evens out differences in pressure. We feel this movement as wind.
111636.m: Wind happens because air flows from high to low pressure.

111637.q: What is the famous experiment called in which horses could not pull apart two hemispheres with the air pumped out?
111637.e: Otto von Guericke pumped the air out of two hemispheres placed together. The air pressure outside pressed them together so hard that even teams of horses could not separate them.
111637.m: The Magdeburg hemispheres show the power of air pressure.

111638.q: Why do your ears pop on a fast cable car ride?
a: The air suddenly gets more humid.
The cable car is too loud.
111638.e: At first the old pressure stays in the middle ear while the pressure outside changes. When the pressure evens out through the Eustachian tube, your ears pop.
111638.m: Ear popping is pressure evening out.

111639.e: A barometer shows the air pressure. If it falls, bad weather often follows; if it rises, the weather usually gets better.

111640.q: How high is the column of mercury in a barometer at normal air pressure at sea level?
111640.e: Normal air pressure balances a column of mercury 760 millimetres high. That is where the old unit “millimetres of mercury” comes from.
111640.m: Normal air pressure holds up 760 millimetres of mercury.

111641.q: How does an aneroid barometer work?
a: A metal box with the air removed changes shape with the air pressure.
A hair stretches with the air pressure.
A paddle wheel turns with the air pressure.
A spirit level tilts with the air pressure.
111641.e: In an aneroid barometer, a metal box with almost no air inside is squeezed more or less. A pointer transfers this movement onto a scale.
111641.m: An aneroid barometer works without any liquid.

111642.q: What do you call a barometer that continuously records the air pressure as a curve?
111642.e: A barograph writes the air pressure with a pen on a turning drum. This shows whether the pressure is rising or falling.
111642.m: A barograph records air pressure as a curve.

111643.q: Roughly how tall would a barometer using water instead of mercury have to be?
111643.e: Water is about 13.6 times lighter than mercury. So it takes a column of water about 10 metres high to balance the air pressure.
111643.m: A water barometer would be as tall as a three-storey house.

111644.q: What does a rapidly falling air pressure on the barometer usually mean?
a: a long spell of fine weather
111644.e: If the pressure falls quickly, a low-pressure area is often approaching. Clouds, rain and wind then become more likely.
111644.m: Falling air pressure often announces worse weather.

111645.q: Which device used by mountaineers works on the same principle as a barometer?
111645.e: Because air pressure falls with height, you can work out the height from the pressure. But a barometric altimeter has to be reset when the weather changes.
111645.m: An altimeter works out height from air pressure.

111646.q: What does the Greek word “baros” in the word barometer mean?
111646.e: “Baros” means weight and “metron” means measure. So the name contains the idea of measuring weight.
111646.m: The word barometer contains the Greek word for weight.

111647.q: What does a barometer show if you carry it up a high mountain?
a: Lower air pressure than in the valley
Higher air pressure than in the valley
Exactly the same air pressure as in the valley
111647.e: The higher you climb, the less air there is above you. That is why the air pressure falls. A famous experiment on the Puy de Dôme mountain in France showed this as early as 1648.
111647.m: On mountains, air pressure is lower than in the valley.

111648.q: Why is a human hair suitable as a sensor in a hygrometer?
a: It gets longer in damp air.
It conducts electricity in the cold.
It gets stiffer in the wind.
It turns darker in the rain.
111648.e: A hair with the grease removed absorbs moisture and stretches a little. This small change in length moves a pointer.
111648.m: Hair gets slightly longer in damp air.

111649.q: What does a relative humidity of 100 per cent mean?
a: The air is saturated with water vapour.
The air consists only of water.
It is raining equally hard everywhere.
111649.e: At 100 per cent, the air cannot take up any more water vapour. Then fog, dew or clouds form.
111649.m: At 100 per cent relative humidity, the air is saturated.

a: It compares a dry thermometer with a wet one.
It weighs a drop of water.
It counts raindrops on a plate.
It measures the colour of the clouds.
111650.e: Water evaporates from the wet thermometer and cools it down. The drier the air, the bigger the temperature difference between the two thermometers.
111650.m: A psychrometer uses the cooling effect of evaporation.

111651.q: What is the temperature called at which the air is saturated with water vapour and dew forms?
111651.e: When air cools down to the dew point, water vapour condenses. That is how dew forms on the grass in the morning, for example.
111651.m: At the dew point, water vapour starts to condense.

111652.q: What happens to the relative humidity when air is warmed without adding any water?
111652.e: Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air. If the amount of water stays the same, the air is less saturated afterwards.

111653.q: What does the Greek word “hygros” in the word hygrometer mean?
111653.e: “Hygros” means damp. So a hygrometer measures how damp the air is.
111653.m: A hygrometer measures the humidity of the air.

111654.e: A hygrometer measures how much water vapour is in the air. This is usually given as a percentage.

111655.e: An anemometer is a wind gauge. It shows how fast the air is moving.
111655.m: An anemometer measures how fast the wind blows.

111656.q: What is the anemometer with three or four spinning half cups called?
111656.e: The wind catches in the open cups and turns the cross. The faster it spins, the stronger the wind.
111656.m: In a cup anemometer, the wind turns small cups.

111657.q: How does an ultrasonic anemometer measure the wind?
a: by how long sound signals take to travel
111657.e: The wind speeds up or slows down sound signals between small transmitters and receivers. From the differences in travel time, the device calculates the strength and direction of the wind.
111657.m: Ultrasonic anemometers have no moving parts.

111658.q: What does the Greek word “anemos” in the word anemometer mean?
111658.e: “Anemos” means wind and “metron” means measure. So an anemometer is a wind measurer.
111658.m: Anemos is the Greek word for wind.

111659.q: Which force on the Beaufort scale describes a hurricane?
111659.e: The Beaufort scale goes from 0 for calm to 12 for hurricane force. It was originally developed for sailing at sea.
111659.m: On the Beaufort scale, 12 is hurricane force.

111660.q: An anemometer shows 10 metres per second. How much is that in kilometres per hour?
111660.e: You multiply metres per second by 3.6. So 10 times 3.6 gives 36 km/h.
111660.m: Metres per second times 3.6 gives kilometres per hour.

111661.q: What do you call a short, violent burst of wind?
111661.e: A gust is a short blast of wind that is much stronger than the average wind. Weather services give peak gusts separately.
111661.m: A gust is a sudden, short blast of wind.

111662.q: In which unit is wind speed often given in aviation and at sea?
111662.e: One knot is one nautical mile per hour, or 1.852 km/h. This unit is common at sea and in aviation.
111662.m: Sailors and pilots measure the wind in knots.

111663.q: Where does the air come from when the foehn brings warm weather to Altdorf or Glarus?
a: From the south over the Alps
From the west, from the Atlantic
111663.e: With the south foehn, air flows from the south over the Alps and drops warm and dry into the valleys on the north side. It is the most common type of foehn in Switzerland.
111663.m: The south foehn blows from the south over the Alps to the north.

111664.q: What is the wall of cloud called that you can see above the main ridge of the Alps during a foehn?
111664.e: The clouds pile up on the windward side and reach over the ridge of the Alps. On the leeward side they dissolve as the air sinks, so a wall forms.
111664.m: During a foehn, a foehn wall rises above the Alps.

111665.q: By about how many degrees does sinking dry air warm up for every 100 metres?
111665.e: As it sinks, the air is squeezed together and warms up by about 1 °C per 100 metres. That is why the foehn is so warm in the valleys.
111665.m: Sinking dry air gets about one degree warmer every 100 metres.

111666.q: What is the weather often like in Ticino during a south foehn?
a: Rain, because air piles up against the Alps
thick low fog with no wind
111666.e: The damp air is held back on the southern side of the Alps and has to rise. As it does, it cools, clouds form and it rains.
111666.m: During a south foehn, it often rains on the southern side of the Alps.

111667.q: What do you call the cloud-free area that forms over the land north of the Alps during a foehn?
111667.e: Because the air sinks on the northern side of the Alps, the clouds dissolve there. This creates a blue window in the sky.
111667.m: The foehn window is a gap in the clouds north of the Alps.

111668.q: What is the weather in Ticino often like when the north foehn is blowing?
111668.e: With the north foehn, the air piles up on the northern side of the Alps and rains out there. In Ticino it comes down dry and warm, and it is sunny and windy.
111668.m: The north foehn brings dry weather to Ticino.

111669.q: Why were there once strict bans on fires in foehn valleys when the foehn was blowing?
a: The warm, dry wind fans fires strongly.
The foehn brings lightning with it.
Water for putting out fires freezes in the foehn.
111669.e: During a foehn, a single spark can quickly start a big fire. In 1861, a fire during a foehn storm destroyed large parts of the town of Glarus.
111669.m: During a foehn, the risk of fire is especially high.

111670.q: Why do the mountains look especially close during a foehn?
a: The air is very dry and clear.
The mountains grow during a foehn.
Thick fog lies over the land.
111670.e: The sinking foehn air is dry and contains hardly any haze. This makes it possible to see very far.
111670.m: During a foehn, you can often see very far.

111671.q: What does the foehn wind usually feel like on the northern side of the Alps?
111671.e: The air rises on the southern side of the Alps and rains out. On the northern side it sinks, warms up and arrives in the valley warm and dry.
111671.m: The foehn is a warm, dry downslope wind.

111672.q: Why does the bise often blow more strongly around Lake Geneva than in eastern Switzerland?
a: The Central Plateau gets narrower towards the south-west.
Lake Geneva makes its own wind.
There are more mountains in Geneva.
111672.e: Between the Jura and the Alps, the Central Plateau narrows towards Geneva. The air is squeezed there and so flows faster.
111672.m: The narrower the Central Plateau, the stronger the bise.

111673.q: Which pressure pattern typically brings the bise to Switzerland?
a: High in the north and low in the south
Low in the north and high in the south
111673.e: When there is a high over northern Europe and a low over the Mediterranean, air flows from the north-east into the Central Plateau. That is the bise.
111673.m: The bise comes with high pressure in the north and low pressure in the south.

111674.q: In western Switzerland, what do you call a bise with thick cloud?
111674.e: With the bise noire, the sky is grey and overcast. With the bise claire, on the other hand, it is sunny and clear.
111674.m: The bise noire brings a grey sky.

111675.q: Why does the bise feel especially cold in winter?
a: The wind quickly takes heat away from the body.
The bise contains ice crystals from space.
The bise lowers the air pressure sharply.
111675.e: Wind keeps carrying away the layer of warm air above your skin. This makes the temperature feel much lower than the thermometer shows.
111675.m: Wind makes cold feel even colder.

111676.q: What can a strong bise cause on the shores of Lake Geneva in winter?
a: thick layers of ice from freezing spray
hail out of a clear sky
111676.e: The bise whips water onto the shore, where it freezes at once in the frost. Trees, benches and even cars get covered in thick ice.
111676.m: Bise and frost can cover the shore of Lake Geneva in ice.

111677.q: What weather does the bise usually bring in summer?
a: dry, rather cool and sunny weather
111677.e: The bise brings dry air from the north-east. So in summer it often makes the weather clear and pleasantly fresh.
111677.m: In summer, the bise usually brings dry, clear weather.

111678.q: What is the effect called that strengthens the bise in the narrow Central Plateau?
111678.e: When a flow is forced through a narrow gap, it has to move faster. This is called the funnel effect.
111678.m: The funnel effect speeds up wind in narrow passages.

111679.q: What are the lines of equal air pressure on a weather map called?
111679.e: Isobars join places with the same air pressure. The Greek “isos” means equal.
111679.m: Isobars join places with the same air pressure.

111680.q: What do isobars lying close together show?
111680.e: When the isobars are close together, the air pressure changes a lot over a short distance. The air then flows quickly and a strong wind blows.
111680.m: The closer the isobars, the stronger the wind.

111681.q: How is a cold front shown on a weather map?
a: as a blue line with triangles
as a red line with semicircles
111681.e: The triangles point in the direction the cold front is moving. Blue stands for the cold air following behind.
111681.m: Cold fronts are blue and have triangles.

111682.q: How is a warm front shown on a weather map?
a: as a red line with semicircles
as a blue line with triangles
111682.e: The red semicircles point in the direction the front is moving. Red stands for the warm air following behind.
111682.m: Warm fronts are red and have semicircles.

111683.q: What weather does a warm front often bring?
111683.e: At a warm front, warm air slowly slides over colder air. This forms wide layers of cloud, from which it often rains steadily for a long time.
111683.m: A warm front often brings long-lasting rain.

111685.q: What weather does a passing cold front often bring?
a: Showers, thunderstorms and a sudden drop in temperature
111685.e: The heavy cold air pushes under the warm air and lifts it quickly. This forms tall heaped clouds with heavy showers, and afterwards it gets cooler.
111685.m: After a cold front, it usually gets much cooler.

111686.q: In German-speaking countries, what does a large T on a weather map stand for?
111686.e: T marks low-pressure areas and H marks high-pressure areas. This lets you quickly spot the most important pressure systems.
111686.m: On German weather maps, T stands for low and H for high.

111687.q: In which direction does air turn around a high-pressure area in the Northern Hemisphere?
111687.e: The air flows out of the high and is deflected by the Earth's rotation. In the Northern Hemisphere, this creates a clockwise turn.
111687.m: Highs turn clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere.

111689.q: During high-pressure weather in winter, what often lies over the Central Plateau for days while it is sunny in the mountains?
111689.e: Cold, damp air stays at the bottom, and above it is warmer. From the mountains, you see the low fog as a sea of fog.
111689.m: In winter, there is often low fog under a high.

111690.q: Which high often brings very cold air to central Europe in winter?
111690.e: Over Russia and Siberia, the air cools down a lot in winter and forms a strong high. From there, icy air flows west.
111690.m: The Russian high brings cold to central Europe in winter.

111691.q: Why are nights often especially cold during high-pressure weather?
a: Without clouds, the ground gives off a lot of heat.
The high pressure cools the air.
The sun shines more weakly at night than usual.
The moon takes heat away from the Earth.
111691.e: Clouds act like a blanket that holds heat in. When the sky is clear, the heat escapes freely into space.
111691.m: Clear nights are usually cold nights.

111692.q: What do you call a strong high that stays in one place for a long time and steers lows around it?
111692.e: A blocking high often stays in the same place for days or weeks. Lows have to move around it, which can lead to heat or drought.
111692.m: A blocking high can control the weather for weeks.

111693.q: In which direction does air turn around a low-pressure area in the Northern Hemisphere?
111693.e: The air flows into the low and is deflected by the Earth's rotation. In the Northern Hemisphere, this creates an anticlockwise turn.
111693.m: Lows turn anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere.

111694.q: Why do low-pressure areas often bring clouds and rain or snow?
a: Because the air rises and cools.
Because the air sinks and dries.
Because they bring dust from the desert.
111694.e: In a low, air rises and cools as it goes. The water vapour condenses into clouds, from which it rains or snows.

111695.q: What is the low-pressure area in the North Atlantic called that strongly affects the weather in Europe?
111695.e: On average, there is a low-pressure area near Iceland. Together with the Azores high, it steers the westerly winds towards Europe.
111695.m: The Icelandic low helps shape the weather in Europe.

111696.q: What do you call a low that forms in summer over land that has heated up strongly?
111696.e: Over land that has heated up a lot, warm air rises and the air pressure at the ground falls. Heat lows like this form in summer over the Iberian Peninsula, for example.
111696.m: A heat low forms when the ground heats up strongly.

111697.q: Which low over northern Italy often brings heavy rain to the southern side of the Alps?
111697.e: Lows often form over the Gulf of Genoa. They carry damp Mediterranean air towards the Alps, which can bring heavy rain to Ticino.
111697.m: A Genoa low often brings a lot of rain to Ticino.

111698.q: Which hurricane-force storm caused great damage in Swiss forests on 26 December 1999?
111698.e: The storm Lothar swept across Switzerland on St Stephen's Day 1999. It blew down millions of trees and caused enormous damage.
111698.m: The storm Lothar raged across Switzerland in 1999.

111699.q: What are highs and lows given in central Europe so that they can be told apart easily?
111699.e: Highs and lows get first names such as Lothar or Burglind. The names are given out in Berlin, and you can even buy a sponsorship for one.
111699.m: Highs and lows have first names.

111700.q: Which two fronts belong to a typical low in the mid-latitudes?
111700.e: At the front of a low like this, warm air pushes forward, and cold air follows behind. This creates a warm front and a cold front.
111700.m: A typical low brings a warm front and a cold front.

111701.q: What do you call the lowest air pressure in the centre of a low?
111701.e: The lower the central pressure, the stronger the low usually is. Storm lows have very low central pressures.
111701.m: A low central pressure often means stormy weather.

111702.q: How is the position of a radiosonde, and with it the wind high up, worked out today?
a: with a compass in the balloon
111702.e: The sonde receives satellite signals and keeps working out its position. From how far it drifts, the wind at every height can be calculated.
111702.m: A radiosonde measures high-altitude wind from its GPS position.

111703.q: Why are radiosondes launched at the same times all over the world?
a: So that all measurements are available at the same time.
So that the balloons do not get lost.
So that aeroplanes can see them.
So that they rise in the moonlight.
111703.e: Weather models need a picture of the whole atmosphere taken as close to the same moment as possible. That is why there are fixed international launch times.
111703.m: Radiosondes are launched at fixed times all over the world.

111704.q: What is the boundary layer between the troposphere and the stratosphere called, which a radiosonde passes through?
111704.e: At the tropopause, the temperature stops falling with height. Above Switzerland it is usually about 10 to 12 kilometres high.
111704.m: The tropopause separates the troposphere and the stratosphere.

111705.q: What temperature does a radiosonde typically measure at about 10 kilometres up?
111705.e: In the troposphere it gets colder with height. At about 10 kilometres up, temperatures are usually around -50 °C.
111705.m: High up in the atmosphere it is freezing cold.

111706.q: Which substance does a special sonde in Payerne regularly measure in the atmosphere?
111706.e: Ozone sondes measure how much ozone there is at different heights. Payerne has one of the longest series of measurements in the world.
111706.m: The ozone layer is also studied in Payerne.

111707.q: A weather balloon rises at 5 metres per second. How long does it take to reach 15 kilometres?
111707.e: 15 kilometres is 15,000 metres. 15,000 divided by 5 gives 3000 seconds, and that is 50 minutes.
111707.m: To find the rising time, divide the height by the rising speed.

111708.q: What can you tell from a radiosonde's temperature profile, for example?
a: the water temperature of the lakes
111708.e: The sonde measures the temperature at every height. If somewhere it gets warmer instead of colder as you go up, that is an inversion.
111708.m: Radiosondes show how temperature changes with height.

111709.q: What lets you forecast thunderstorms for the next few hours especially well?
111709.e: Weather radar shows where it is raining right now and where the storm cells are moving. This makes it possible to give fairly accurate warnings for the next few hours.
111709.m: Radar images help forecast thunderstorms in the short term.

111710.q: What does a 30 per cent chance of rain mean?
a: In 3 out of 10 similar cases, it rains.
It rains for 30 per cent of the day.
30 per cent of the country gets wet.
111710.e: The probability tells you how often it rains in one place with this kind of weather. So at 30 per cent, it usually stays dry.
111710.m: With a 30 per cent chance of rain, it will probably stay dry.

111711.q: What does the butterfly effect mean in weather forecasting?
a: Small changes can have big consequences
More butterflies fly when it is sunny
Wind is created by wing beats
111711.e: The meteorologist Edward Lorenz showed that tiny differences in the starting values can lead to completely different results. That is why the weather can only be forecast well a few days ahead.
111711.m: The butterfly effect shows how sensitive the weather is to small changes.

111712.q: What is a farmer's weather saying?
a: An old saying about the weather
A game played in the countryside
111712.e: Farmers' sayings are old rhymes and sayings that farmers used to try to predict the weather, for example about the Seven Sleepers' Day on 27 June. Some are roughly right, but many are not.
111712.m: Farmers' sayings are old weather sayings.

111713.q: What are the European weather satellites called that seem to stand still high above the equator?
111713.e: The Meteosat satellites circle as fast as the Earth turns. That is why they always watch the same area with Europe and Africa.
111713.m: Meteosat satellites keep watch over Europe from space.

111714.q: Why does Switzerland need weather models with an especially fine grid?
a: So that mountains and valleys are shown accurately.
So that the calculation finishes faster.
So that there is less data.
So that the model needs no measurements.
111714.e: The finer the grid, the more accurately mountains, valleys and lakes are shown in the model. This is especially important in Switzerland's mountainous landscape.
111714.m: Mountains need especially accurate weather models.

111715.q: What can you see with a weather radar?
a: Where it is raining or snowing right now
How high the air pressure is
111715.e: Radar sends out waves that are bounced back by raindrops, snowflakes and hail. MeteoSwiss runs five such radars.
111715.m: Weather radars show where it is raining or snowing.

111716.q: What is the main job of phagocytes in the body?
111716.e: Phagocytes surround bacteria, dead cells and foreign substances and break them down inside themselves. In this way they clear away intruders and cell remains.
111716.m: Phagocytes swallow germs and break them down.

111717.q: Where in the body are phagocytes found?
a: In the blood and in the tissues
111717.e: Phagocytes travel in the blood and move into the tissues when needed. There they eat germs and cell remains.
111717.m: Phagocytes patrol the blood and tissues.

111718.q: Apart from germs, what else do phagocytes eat?
111718.e: Phagocytes also clear away dead cells and cell debris. They are the body's cleaning team.
111718.m: Phagocytes also clear away cell remains.

111719.q: How does a phagocyte make a germ harmless?
a: It surrounds it and digests it
It stabs it with a spike
It flushes it out of the body
111719.e: The phagocyte wraps its outer layer around the germ and encloses it in a little bubble. There it is broken down by enzymes.

111720.q: Which group of blood cells do phagocytes belong to?
111720.e: Phagocytes are part of the white blood cells, the leukocytes. These cells are responsible for defence.

111721.q: Why is there often pus when a wound is infected?
a: It is made of dead defence cells and germs
It is fat that has leaked out
111721.e: Pus contains many white blood cells that have fought against the germs, along with germs and cell remains.
111721.m: Pus shows that defence cells have been fighting.

111722.q: How do phagocytes work together with other defence cells?
a: They show them parts of the germ
They eat the other defence cells
111722.e: Phagocytes display fragments of the germs they have eaten on their surface. That way other defence cells recognise the enemy and can fight it in a targeted way.

111723.q: Where do phagocytes move to when bacteria multiply in a wound?
a: Out of the blood into the wound
111723.e: With inflammation, phagocytes leave the blood vessels and move to the wound. There they eat the bacteria.

111724.q: Which body fluid is filtered in the lymph nodes?
111724.e: Lymph is a pale fluid from the tissues. On its way back into the blood, it flows through lymph nodes, which filter out germs.

111725.q: Why do lymph nodes often swell during an infection?
a: Because defence cells multiply strongly there
Because they store water for later
111725.e: When defence cells in the lymph node recognise a germ, they multiply quickly. This makes the lymph node bigger and sometimes tender.
111725.m: Swollen lymph nodes show that the body's defences are working.

111726.q: Where can you often easily feel swollen lymph nodes when you have a cold?
a: On the top of the foot
111726.e: There are many lymph nodes in the neck that filter the lymph from the head and throat. That is why you can often feel them when you have a cold.
111726.m: With a sore throat, the lymph nodes in the neck are often swollen.

111727.q: Roughly how many lymph nodes does an adult have?
111727.e: A person has around 600 to 700 lymph nodes. Many of them are in the neck, the armpits, the groin and the abdomen.
111727.m: Humans have a few hundred lymph nodes.

111728.q: Which defence cells are found in especially large numbers in the lymph nodes?
111728.e: Lymphocytes, that is B cells and T cells, gather in the lymph nodes. There they meet germs and are activated.
111728.m: In lymph nodes, many lymphocytes wait for germs.

111729.q: Which organ system do the lymph nodes belong to?
111729.e: Lymph nodes, lymph vessels and the spleen belong to the lymphatic system. It mainly serves defence and the removal of tissue fluid.
111729.m: Lymph nodes are part of the lymphatic system.

111730.q: What shape are lymph nodes typically?
111730.e: Lymph nodes are usually bean-shaped and a few millimetres to about one centimetre in size. They are embedded in the tissue.
111730.m: Lymph nodes look like small beans.

111731.q: What are the vessels called that bring lymph to the lymph nodes?
111731.e: Lymph vessels collect fluid from the tissues and lead it through the lymph nodes. Finally, the lymph flows into the veins.
111731.m: Lymph vessels carry lymph through the lymph nodes.

a: At the back of the throat on each side
At the top of the nasal cavity
Low down in the voice box
111732.e: The tonsils lie on the left and right between the arches of the palate, where the mouth meets the throat. You can see them when you open your mouth wide.
111732.m: The tonsils sit on the left and right at the back of the throat.

111733.q: What do you often feel especially strongly with tonsillitis?
a: A stabbing pain in the knee
111733.e: The inflamed tonsils are swollen and red. That is why swallowing hurts most of all, and there is often a fever too.
111733.m: Tonsillitis gives you a sore throat when swallowing.

111734.q: Why are tonsils sometimes removed in an operation?
a: Because they get inflamed very often
Because they push the teeth out of place
111734.e: If someone gets tonsillitis very often, their tonsils can be taken out. The body still has plenty of other defence cells.
111734.m: If they get inflamed very often, the tonsils are sometimes removed.

111735.q: How many tonsils (palatine tonsils) does a person normally have?
111735.e: There is one tonsil on the left and one on the right side of the throat. There are also other tonsils, such as the adenoids.

111736.q: What job do the tonsils do?
a: Recognising germs from the mouth and nose early
Controlling the pitch of the voice
111736.e: The tonsils are made of lymphatic tissue. They come into contact early with germs from the air we breathe and from food, and they trigger a defence.
111736.m: The tonsils are guards at the entrance to the mouth and throat.

111737.q: What kind of tissue are the tonsils mainly made of?
111737.e: The tonsils contain a great many defence cells. That is why they belong to the immune system and help to recognise germs early.
111737.m: The tonsils are made of defence tissue.

111738.q: What are enlarged adenoids in children commonly called in German, even though it is not quite correct?
111738.e: Enlarged adenoids can make breathing through the nose difficult. In everyday German they are called “polyps”, even though they are not real polyps.
111738.m: Enlarged adenoids are often called polyps.

111739.q: What does the doctor use to treat tonsillitis caused by bacteria?
111739.e: Antibiotics work against bacteria. They do not help against viruses, so the doctor often first does a test to see which germs are the cause.
111739.m: Antibiotics help against bacteria, not viruses.

a: A defence reaction of the body to something harmful
A special kind of broken bone
An inherited disease you are born with
111740.e: Inflammation happens when the body reacts to germs, injuries or foreign substances. It is meant to limit the damage and start healing.
111740.m: Inflammation is a protective reaction of the body.

111741.q: What is inflammation called that lasts for months or even years?
111741.e: Acute inflammation starts suddenly and usually dies down after a few days. If it lasts a long time, it is called chronic inflammation.

111742.q: Which is NOT a typical sign of inflammation?
111742.e: Typical signs of inflammation are redness, warmth, swelling, pain and limited function. The spot becomes warm, not cold.
111742.m: Inflamed spots are red, warm, swollen and painful.

111743.q: Why does an inflamed spot become warm?
a: Because more blood flows to it
Because the skin there gets thinner
111743.e: With inflammation, the blood vessels widen. More warm blood flows into the area, which therefore feels warm.
111743.m: More blood flow makes inflamed spots warm.

a: Because fluid leaks from the blood vessels into the tissue
Because air gets under the skin
Because the muscles there get thicker
111744.e: The walls of the small blood vessels become leakier. Fluid and defence cells get into the tissue, which makes it swell.
111744.m: Leaking fluid makes inflamed tissue swell.

111745.q: Which ending do many medical names for inflammations have?
111745.e: Examples are bronchitis and arthritis. The ending “-oma”, on the other hand, often stands for a growth, and “-algia” for pain.

111746.e: The ending “-itis” stands for inflammation. In bronchitis, the branches of the windpipe are inflamed.
111746.m: Bronchitis is an inflammation of the bronchi.

111747.q: Which cells move into the tissue during inflammation to fight germs?
111747.e: White blood cells are part of the body's defences. During inflammation they move out of the blood vessels into the tissue and fight germs.
111747.m: White blood cells fight germs during inflammation.

111748.q: Why does an inflamed spot often hurt?
a: Messenger substances and the swelling irritate the pain nerves
111748.e: During inflammation, messenger substances are released and the tissue swells. Both irritate the nerves, which is why the spot hurts.

111749.q: What is pus mainly made of?
a: Dead defence cells, germs and bits of tissue
Fat and oil from the skin
111749.e: Pus forms when many defence cells die while fighting bacteria. Together with germs and broken-down tissue they form a thick fluid.
111749.m: Pus is mainly made of dead defence cells.

111750.q: What is an enclosed collection of pus in a newly formed cavity in the tissue called?
111750.e: In an abscess, tissue is broken down and a cavity full of pus forms. A haematoma, on the other hand, is a bruise.
111750.m: An abscess is a cavity of pus in the tissue.

111751.q: What is a pus-filled inflammation of a hair follicle and the area around it called?
111751.e: A boil usually develops from bacteria that get into a hair follicle. A painful, pus-filled lump forms.
111751.m: A boil is an inflamed, pus-filled hair follicle.

111752.e: Pus is usually yellowish to greenish and cloudy. The colour comes from the many cells and their parts.
111752.m: Pus is usually yellowish and cloudy.

111753.q: Which bacteria are among the most common causes of pus?
111753.e: Staphylococcus aureus is one of the main causes of pus-filled skin and wound infections. Lactic acid bacteria, on the other hand, are used for yoghurt, for example.

111754.q: Why should you not squeeze a pus-filled spot with dirty fingers?
111754.e: When you squeeze, bacteria can get deeper into the tissue. Then the inflammation can get bigger.
111754.m: It is better not to squeeze pus-filled spots.

111755.q: Which cells fight bacteria during inflammation and form pus in the process?
111755.e: White blood cells move to the inflammation and eat bacteria. Many die in the process and form pus together with the germs.
111755.m: Pus forms from dead white blood cells.

111756.q: What is a small blister on the skin filled with pus called?
111756.e: A pustule is a pus blister, as found in acne, for example. A papule is a small bump without pus.
111756.m: A pustule is a pus blister.

111757.q: What job do the memory cells of the immune system do?
a: Recognise a germ again and fight it quickly
111757.e: Memory cells stay in the body after an infection. If they meet the same germ again, they immediately start a strong defence.
111757.m: Memory cells remember germs that were fought before.

111758.q: Which blood cells do memory cells belong to?
111758.e: White blood cells are the body's defence cells. Memory cells are a special kind of them.
111758.m: Memory cells are white blood cells.

111759.q: Why do you usually get chickenpox only once in your life?
a: Memory cells recognise the virus the next time
The virus only occurs in children
The skin becomes impenetrable with age
The virus dies out in summer
111759.e: After the first illness, long-lasting immunity remains. Memory cells make sure that a new infection is usually fought off without any signs of illness.
111759.m: Anyone who has had chickenpox is usually protected for life.

111760.q: How does a vaccination make use of memory cells?
a: The body makes them without really getting ill
It kills all the old memory cells
It turns memory cells into red blood cells
It prevents memory cells from forming
111760.e: A vaccine contains weakened or killed germs or parts of them. The immune system reacts to them and creates memory cells.
111760.m: A vaccination trains the immune memory.

111761.q: Where in the body are the white blood cells made from which memory cells develop?
111761.e: All blood cells, including white blood cells, are made in the red bone marrow. Some of them later become memory cells.
111761.m: Defence cells are made in the bone marrow.

111762.q: How long can some memory cells survive in the body?
111762.e: Many memory cells are very long-lived. That is why getting over an illness or having a vaccination often protects you for a very long time.
111762.m: Memory cells can live for decades.

111763.q: How does the immune system react the second time it meets the same germ?
a: Exactly the same as the first time
111763.e: The first time, the defences need a few days. The second time, the memory cells recognise the germ immediately and the defence starts faster and more strongly.
111763.m: The second time, the body defends itself faster.

111764.q: What does a booster vaccination do?
a: It raises the number of memory cells and antibodies again
It replaces the making of red blood cells
111764.e: With some vaccinations, the protection fades over time. Another dose refreshes the immune memory.
111764.m: A booster vaccination strengthens the immune memory.

111765.q: What kind of organ is the thymus?
111765.e: Defence cells are trained in the thymus. So it serves the body's defence, not digestion, the senses or excretion.
111765.m: The thymus is an organ of the immune system.

111766.q: Which defence cells mature in the thymus?
111766.e: In the thymus these cells are trained and mature into working defence cells. They are also named after this organ.
111766.m: T cells mature in the thymus.

111767.q: What would happen if a child were born without a working thymus?
111767.e: Without a thymus, no mature T cells can form. The body then lacks an important part of its defences, and infections become very dangerous.
111767.m: Without a thymus, the body lacks an important part of its defences.

111768.q: How does the thymus change over the course of life?
a: It shrinks and partly turns into fatty tissue
It keeps growing into old age
It turns to bone and becomes a rib
It moves from the chest into the abdomen
111768.e: The thymus is large and active in children. In adults it gets smaller and smaller and is mostly replaced by fat.

111769.q: Where do the immature precursor cells come from that mature in the thymus?
111769.e: All blood cells are made in the bone marrow. Some of the precursors of the lymphocytes travel from there through the blood to the thymus.
111769.m: The precursors of the thymus cells come from the bone marrow.

111770.q: What do T cells learn in the thymus?
a: To tell the body's own cells from foreign ones
111770.e: In the thymus, T cells that would attack the body itself are sorted out. The cells that remain only fight foreign substances.
111770.m: In the thymus, T cells learn to spare the body itself.

111771.q: In cooking, what is the thymus of a calf known as?
111771.e: Veal sweetbreads, called Kalbsmilken in Switzerland, are the thymus of young calves. Tripe, on the other hand, is part of a cow's stomach.
111771.m: Veal sweetbreads are the thymus of a calf.

111772.q: How many lobes does the thymus have?
111772.e: The thymus has a left and a right lobe. These are divided into many small lobules.

111773.q: What is typical of the non-specific defence?
a: It works immediately against many different germs
It is only aimed at a single germ
It only starts after several weeks
It only comes from a vaccination
111773.e: The non-specific defence does not tell individual germs apart precisely. Instead it reacts very quickly, within the first minutes to hours.
111773.m: The non-specific defence reacts immediately, but not in a targeted way.

111774.q: What is the non-specific defence also called?
111774.e: You are born with the non-specific defence. The specific defence, on the other hand, is only acquired during life.

111775.q: Which substance in the stomach kills many swallowed germs?
111775.e: Stomach juice contains hydrochloric acid and is very acidic. Many bacteria do not survive this acidic environment.

111776.q: How do tears protect the eye from bacteria?
a: They wash germs away and contain a substance that attacks bacteria
They cool the eye down a lot
They colour the bacteria so they can be seen
111776.e: Tears rinse dirt and germs out of the eye. They also contain an enzyme that destroys the walls of bacteria.
111776.m: Tears are part of the body's own defences.

111777.q: How does healthy skin protect against germs?
a: It forms a tight barrier to the outside
It makes antibodies against every virus
It lets T cells mature in it
It filters the lymph from the tissue
111777.e: The outer horny layer of the skin cannot be penetrated by most germs. Only through injuries can they get in easily.
111777.m: Unbroken skin keeps most germs out.

111778.q: How can fever help the body's defences?
a: It slows down some germs and speeds up defence processes
It replaces the making of antibodies
It stops you ever getting ill again
111778.e: Many germs multiply less well at a raised temperature. At the same time, some defence reactions run faster.
111778.m: Fever helps the body's own defences.

111779.q: Which cells of the innate defence kill body cells infected by viruses?
111779.e: Natural killer cells recognise sick body cells by changed features on their surface. They do not need any previous training for this.
111779.m: Natural killer cells kill infected cells immediately.

111780.q: How do harmless bacteria on the skin and in the gut protect against germs?
a: They take up the space and food the germs need
They make antibodies against the germs
They let T cells mature in the gut
111780.e: The natural bacterial flora covers the skin and gut thickly. This leaves harmful germs hardly any space or food to settle.
111780.m: Useful bacteria crowd out harmful germs.

111781.q: What is typical of the specific defence?
a: It is aimed specifically at one particular germ
It works the same against all germs
It consists only of the skin
It only works in the stomach
111781.e: The specific defence recognises exact features of a germ. For this it needs more time the first time it meets it.
111781.m: The specific defence fights germs in a targeted way.

111782.q: What does the specific defence make that is aimed at one particular germ?
111782.e: Certain white blood cells make antibodies that fit exactly one germ. Stomach acid, skin oil and tears, on the other hand, work the same against all germs.
111782.m: Antibodies fight germs in a targeted way.

111783.q: What is a foreign substance called against which the body makes antibodies?
111783.e: An antigen is a feature, for example on the surface of a bacterium, that the immune system recognises. Antibodies bind exactly to this feature.

111784.q: What shape are antibodies in simplified drawings?
111784.e: An antibody consists of four protein chains that together form a Y. The binding sites for the antigen are on the two arms.

111785.q: By which principle does an antibody fit its antigen?
111785.e: An antibody only fits one particular antigen, just as a key only fits one lock. That is why the defence is specific.
111785.m: Antibody and antigen fit like a key and a lock.

111786.q: Which T cells kill virus-infected body cells in a targeted way?
111786.e: Killer T cells, also called cytotoxic T cells, recognise infected cells by their antigens. Then they make them die.
111786.m: Killer T cells destroy infected body cells.

111787.q: What job do helper T cells do?
a: They activate and direct other defence cells
111787.e: Helper T cells release messenger substances that activate B cells and killer cells. They are something like the command centre of the defence.
111787.m: Helper T cells coordinate the specific defence.

111788.q: The first time you meet a germ, roughly how long does it take for the specific defence to work fully?
111788.e: First, matching lymphocytes have to be found, activated and multiplied. The first time, this takes about one to two weeks.
111788.m: The first specific defence needs a few days to weeks.

111789.q: What is the mucus on the linings of the airways for?
111789.e: Particles and germs that are breathed in stick in the sticky mucus. That way they do not get deeper into the lungs.
111789.m: Mucus traps germs in the airways.

111790.q: Which tiny hairs move mucus in the airways towards the throat?
111790.e: Cilia move like a waving carpet and push the mucus upwards. There it is swallowed or coughed up.
111790.m: Cilia carry mucus out of the airways.

111791.q: Which part of the body is lined inside with mucous membrane?
111791.e: Mucous membranes line inner cavities that are connected to the outside world, such as the nose, mouth and gut. Fingertips, soles of the feet and the scalp are covered by normal skin.
111791.m: The nose, mouth and gut are lined with mucous membrane.

111792.q: Which defence substances give the mucous membranes extra protection from germs?
111792.e: There are special antibodies in saliva, tears and gut mucus. They stop germs from settling on the mucous membranes.

111793.q: Which reflex shoots irritants and germs out of the nose?
111793.e: Irritation of the lining of the nose triggers a sneeze. Air is pushed out through the nose and mouth at high speed.
111793.m: Sneezing cleans irritants out of the nose.

111794.q: Which reflex clears mucus from the bronchi?
111794.e: When you cough, air is forced strongly out of the lungs. This carries mucus with germs out of the lower airways.
111794.m: Coughing clears mucus from the bronchi.

111795.q: What is an inflammation of the lining of the nose called in everyday language?
111795.e: With a runny nose, the lining of the nose is inflamed and makes a lot of mucus. Experts call this rhinitis.
111795.m: A runny nose is an inflammation of the lining of the nose.

111796.q: What protects the stomach lining from being attacked by its own acid?
111796.e: The stomach lining makes sticky mucus and bicarbonate. This layer keeps the acid away from the cells.
111796.m: Mucus protects the stomach from its own acid.

111797.q: What is the mucous membrane called that covers the white of the eye and the inside of the eyelids?
111797.e: The conjunctiva is a thin, see-through mucous membrane. If it is inflamed, this is called conjunctivitis.
111797.m: The conjunctiva is the mucous membrane of the eye.

111798.q: What is meant by herd immunity?
a: Protection of people who are not immune because many others are
Immunity that only occurs in farm animals
Protection from living in a big city
111798.e: If enough people are immune, a germ hardly finds any new chances to spread. That way people without their own protection are also protected indirectly.
111798.m: Herd immunity also protects people who are not immune themselves.

111799.q: Roughly how high must the share of immune people be for measles to create herd immunity?
111799.e: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases of all. That is why very high immunity is needed in the population, around 95 percent.
111799.m: Almost everyone has to be immune to measles.

111800.q: Why is an especially high share of immune people needed for measles?
a: Because there is no vaccine against measles
111800.e: Without immunity in the population, one person with measles can infect a great many others. The more contagious a disease is, the higher the threshold needed.
111800.m: The more contagious a disease, the more immune people are needed.

111801.q: A sick person infects 2 people, and each of them infects 2 more. How many people are infected in this second round?
111801.e: In the first round, 2 people are infected. Each of them infects 2 more: 2 times 2 makes 4. That is how a disease spreads very quickly without protection.
111801.m: Without protection, the number of sick people multiplies with every round.

111802.q: The threshold for herd immunity is calculated, in simplified form, as 1 minus 1/R0. What percentage do you get when R0 = 4?
111802.e: 1 minus 1/4 = 1 minus 0.25 = 0.75. So about 75 percent of the population must be immune.
111802.m: The bigger R0 is, the higher the threshold for herd immunity.

111803.q: Which disease was declared eradicated in 1980 thanks to worldwide vaccination programmes?
111803.e: The World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1980. So far it is the only human infectious disease to have been wiped out.
111803.m: Smallpox was wiped out by vaccination.

111804.q: What can happen if the vaccination rate falls below the necessary threshold?
a: The germ then dies out immediately
111804.e: If too few people are immune, the germ again finds enough chains of infection. Then a disease can spread again.
111804.m: If the vaccination rate falls, new outbreaks threaten.

111805.q: In a population with herd immunity, when does a disease start to decline?
a: When each sick person infects fewer than one person on average
When each sick person infects fewer than ten people on average
When each sick person infects fewer than five people on average
When each sick person infects fewer than a hundred people on average
111805.e: If each sick person infects fewer than one other person on average, the cases become fewer each time. The chains of infection then break off.
111805.m: A disease dies down when each sick person infects fewer than one other person.

111806.q: What is meant by the incubation period?
a: The time from infection to the first symptoms
The whole length of an illness
The time you spend in hospital
The time from the symptoms to recovery
111806.e: The incubation period starts when a germ gets into the body. It ends when the first signs of illness appear.
111806.m: The incubation period lies between infection and the start of illness.

111807.q: Roughly how long is the incubation period for chickenpox?
111807.e: With chickenpox, it usually takes around 14 to 16 days until the rash appears. The range is about 8 to 28 days.
111807.m: Chickenpox breaks out about two weeks after infection.

111808.q: How long is the incubation period for real flu usually?
111808.e: With influenza, the symptoms often start just one to two days after infection. That is why a flu wave can spread very quickly.
111808.m: Flu breaks out only a few days after infection.

111809.q: Why can diseases already spread during the incubation period?
a: Because you are sometimes contagious before you feel ill
Because germs grow through the air during this time
Because the body then has no defence cells
Because you always have a fever during this time
111809.e: With some diseases, you already give off germs before symptoms appear. You do not notice the infection yet and pass it on without knowing.
111809.m: Some sick people are contagious before they have symptoms.

111810.q: What happens in the body during the incubation period?
111810.e: In this phase, the germs multiply until there are enough of them to cause symptoms. At the same time, the immune system begins to react.
111810.m: During the incubation period, the germs multiply unnoticed.

111811.q: Which disease often has an especially long incubation period of several weeks to months?
111811.e: With rabies, the virus travels slowly along the nerves to the brain. That is why it usually takes weeks to months until the first symptoms appear.
111811.m: Rabies can stay unnoticed in the body for a very long time.

111812.q: With which illness do the symptoms often start just a few hours after infection?
111812.e: In food poisoning caused by bacterial toxins, the poisons act directly. That is why nausea and vomiting often start after just a few hours.
111812.m: Bacterial toxins in food act after just a few hours.

111813.q: With measles, roughly how long does it take from infection to the first signs of illness?
111813.e: With measles, the first symptoms such as fever and a runny nose usually appear about 8 to 10 days after infection. The typical rash follows a few days later.
111813.m: Measles begins about ten days after infection.

111814.q: With infectious diseases, what is the length of a quarantine often based on?
a: The weather over the next few days
The age of the person affected
The day of the week of the infection
111814.e: A quarantine should last until you can be sure that no illness will break out. That is why it is based on the incubation period.
111814.m: The length of a quarantine depends on the incubation period.

111815.q: Roughly what wavelength range is the light that humans can see?
111815.e: The eye detects electromagnetic waves from about 380 to 780 nanometres. A nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre.
111815.m: Visible light has wavelengths of a few hundred nanometres.

111816.q: Which colour has the longest wavelength in the visible spectrum?
111816.e: Red light has wavelengths of around 700 nanometres. It is at the long-wave end of the visible spectrum.
111816.m: Red is the visible colour with the longest wavelength.

111817.q: Which colour has the shortest wavelength in the visible spectrum?
111817.e: Violet light is around 400 nanometres, at the short-wave end. After it comes invisible radiation.
111817.m: Violet is the visible colour with the shortest wavelength.

111818.q: Which device splits up and measures the spectrum of light?
111818.e: A spectrometer splits light into its wavelengths with a prism or grating. This measures which colours are present and how strongly.
111818.m: A spectrometer measures the spectrum of light.

111819.q: What kind of wave is light?
