111819.e: Light is an electromagnetic wave, like radio waves or X-rays. Unlike sound, it needs no medium and also travels in a vacuum.

111820.q: What do you call light that consists of only one single wavelength?
111820.e: Monochromatic means “single-coloured”. Laser light comes very close to this ideal, while sunlight contains many wavelengths.

111821.q: What do you call a spectrum in which all colours merge into each other without gaps?
111821.e: Hot solid objects, such as the filament of a light bulb, give off a continuous spectrum. No colours are missing from it.
111821.m: A continuous spectrum contains all colours without gaps.

111822.q: What do you call a spectrum of separate coloured lines, as shown by glowing gases?
111822.e: Glowing gases only give off very particular wavelengths. Each chemical element has its own lines, like a fingerprint.
111822.m: Glowing gases produce a line spectrum.

111823.q: In split sunlight you can see fine dark lines. What do they tell researchers?
a: Which substances the sun is made of
Exactly how old the sun is
How far away the moon is
When it will rain on Earth
111823.e: Gases in the sun's atmosphere absorb very particular colours. Each element has its own lines, so you can tell what the sun is made of.
111823.m: Dark lines in sunlight reveal what the sun is made of.

111824.q: What is meant by dispersion of light?
a: that different colours are refracted by different amounts
that light is reflected by a mirror
that light is absorbed by black surfaces
that light is focused by a magnifying glass
111824.e: The refraction of light depends on its wavelength. So the colours are bent by different amounts when passing into glass or water, and they separate.
111824.m: In dispersion, colours are refracted by different amounts.

111825.q: Which object can split white light into its colours?
111825.e: In a prism, light is refracted on the way in and out. Because each colour is bent by a different amount, the light fans out.
111825.m: A prism fans white light out into colours.

111826.q: Which property of a substance depends on the wavelength of light in dispersion?
111826.e: The refractive index tells you how strongly a substance refracts light. In dispersion it is slightly different for each colour.
111826.m: In dispersion, the refractive index depends on the colour.

111827.q: Which natural phenomenon is caused by dispersion of sunlight in water droplets?
111827.e: In raindrops, sunlight is refracted, reflected and split into colours. This creates a coloured arc.
111827.m: A rainbow is caused by light splitting in raindrops.

111828.q: Where must the sun be for you to see a rainbow?
a: directly in front of the observer
111828.e: The light is reflected back in the drops. So you see a rainbow when the sun is behind you and rain is falling in front of you.
111828.m: To see a rainbow, the sun must be behind you.

111829.q: What shape is a rainbow if you can see all of it, for example from a plane?
111829.e: The rainbow forms at a fixed angle around the point opposite the sun. From the ground, the horizon usually hides the lower part of the circle.
111829.m: A rainbow is really a full circle.

111830.q: How is the order of colours in a secondary rainbow different from the main rainbow?
111830.e: In the secondary rainbow, light is reflected twice inside the drops. This reverses the order of the colours.
111830.m: In the secondary rainbow the colours are reversed.

111831.q: What do you often see at the edges of an image from simple lenses, because they bend colours by different amounts?
111831.e: A lens bends blue light slightly more than red. So the colours don't meet at exactly the same place, and coloured fringes appear at the edge.
111831.m: Simple lenses often show coloured edges.

111832.q: Why does a cut diamond sparkle in many colours?
a: Because it strongly refracts light and splits it into colours
Because it produces its own light inside
Because it contains small coloured specks
Because it stores sunlight like heat
111832.e: Diamond has a high refractive index and strong dispersion. Thanks to the cut, light is refracted several times and split into colours.
111832.m: A diamond splits light into colours especially strongly.

111833.q: Which colour forms when red, green and blue light are mixed equally brightly?
111833.e: In additive mixing, coloured lights are laid on top of each other. All three primary colours together make white light.
111833.m: Red, green and blue together make white light.

111834.q: From which three colours of light does a screen mix all other colours?
111834.e: Each pixel has a red, a green and a blue tiny light. Depending on their brightness, all colours are made from them.
111834.m: Screens mix their colours from red, green and blue.

111835.q: How does a screen produce the colour orange?
a: lots of red, some green and no blue
lots of blue, some green and no red
equal amounts of red, green and blue
111835.e: Orange lies between red and yellow. So red shines strongly, green a little less and blue not at all.
111835.m: On a screen, orange comes from lots of red and some green.

111836.q: Which colour forms when you mix red and green light?
111836.e: In additive mixing, red and green light together make yellow. With watercolours, the same mix would give brown instead.
111836.m: Red and green light make yellow.

111837.q: Which colour forms when you mix green and blue light?
111837.e: Green and blue light together make a bright turquoise blue. This colour is called cyan.
111837.m: Green and blue light make cyan.

111838.q: Where is additive colour mixing used in everyday life?
111838.e: Screens and projectors make colours by letting coloured light shine at different brightnesses. Watercolours, fabric dyes and felt tips, on the other hand, mix colourings.
111838.m: Screens mix their colours from light.

111839.q: Why is colour mixing with light called “additive”?
a: Because light is added and the mix gets brighter
Because you may only use two colours
111839.e: With each extra colour of light, more light reaches the eye. So the mixed colour is brighter than the single colours.
111839.m: Additive means that light is added together.

111840.q: In additive colour mixing, which colour do you see when none of the three lamps is on?
111840.e: Without light nothing reaches the eye, and you see black. So additive mixing starts from black.

111841.q: What are the three primary colours of subtractive colour mixing?
111841.e: For colourings and filters, cyan, magenta and yellow are used. Each of these colours absorbs part of white light.
111841.m: The subtractive primary colours are cyan, magenta and yellow.

111842.q: Which colour forms in subtractive mixing of cyan and yellow?
111842.e: Cyan absorbs red light, yellow absorbs blue light. Green light is left over.
111842.m: Cyan and yellow make green subtractively.

111843.q: Which colour forms in subtractive mixing of magenta and yellow?
111843.e: Magenta absorbs green light, yellow absorbs blue light. Only red light is reflected.
111843.m: Magenta and yellow make red subtractively.

111844.q: Which colour forms in subtractive mixing of cyan and magenta?
111844.e: Cyan absorbs red, magenta absorbs green. Blue light is left over.
111844.m: Cyan and magenta make blue subtractively.

111845.q: Ideally, what forms when cyan, magenta and yellow are printed on top of each other?
111845.e: Together, the three colourings absorb all visible light. Ideally nothing is reflected any more, and you see black.
111845.m: All three subtractive primary colours together make black.

111846.q: Why is colour mixing with colourings called “subtractive”?
a: Because each colouring absorbs part of the light
Because more and more light is added
Because the colours glow by themselves
Because the colours are thinned with water
111846.e: Each colouring removes certain colours from white light. The more colourings you mix, the less light is left and the darker it gets.
111846.m: Subtractive means that colourings take light away.

111847.q: What does a red tomato look like if you light it only with green light?
111847.e: The tomato mainly reflects red light and absorbs green. If only green light falls on it, hardly any light comes back, and it looks dark.
111847.m: An object can only reflect colours that are in the light.

111848.q: In which activity is subtractive colour mixing used?
111848.e: When painting, colourings that absorb parts of the light are mixed. Stage lights and projectors, on the other hand, mix light.
111848.m: Painting with colourings means mixing subtractively.

111849.q: What do the letters RGB stand for?
111849.e: RGB stands for red, green and blue. Colours on screens are described using these three colours of light.
111849.m: RGB stands for red, green and blue.

111850.q: How many bits are needed to represent the 256 brightness levels of a colour channel?
111850.e: 2 to the power of 8 is 256. So 8 bits are enough for the values 0 to 255.

111851.q: How many colours can be shown with 256 levels each for red, green and blue?
111851.e: You multiply the levels of the three channels: 256 times 256 times 256 gives 16,777,216. That is about 16.7 million colours.
111851.m: Three channels of 256 levels give about 16.7 million colours.

111852.q: Which RGB value gives pure red on a screen?
111852.e: The three numbers are in the order red, green, blue. For pure red, only the first channel shines at full strength.
111852.m: In an RGB value, the first number stands for red.

111853.q: What colour is the RGB value (128, 128, 128)?
111853.e: If all three channels shine equally, but only about half as bright as possible, a medium grey forms. Equal values for red, green and blue always give a shade of grey.
111853.m: Equal values for red, green and blue give grey.

111854.q: What colour is the RGB value (255, 255, 0)?
111854.e: Red and green shine fully, blue is off. Red and green light together make yellow.
111854.m: Full red and full green make yellow on a screen.

111855.q: What colour is the hex code #0000FF?
111855.e: A hex code gives red, green and blue with two characters each. FF is the maximum value of 255, here only for blue.
111855.m: In a hex code the last two characters stand for blue.

111856.q: What does a single pixel on a colour screen consist of?
a: a red, a green and a blue sub-pixel
a cyan, a magenta and a yellow sub-pixel
a black and a white sub-pixel
111856.e: Each pixel has three sub-pixels in red, green and blue. Seen from close up, for example with a magnifying glass, you can make them out.
111856.m: A screen pixel is made of three coloured sub-pixels.

111857.q: Which colour does the K in the CMYK colour model stand for?
111857.e: K stands for “key”, the key colour in printing. This means black.
111857.m: The K in CMYK stands for black.

111858.q: What colour appears on white paper with the CMYK value 0 % cyan, 0 % magenta, 0 % yellow and 0 % black?
111858.e: At 0 per cent no ink is printed at all. So you only see the white paper.
111858.m: Without ink the paper stays white.

111859.q: What are the tiny dots called that a printed colour picture is made of?
111859.e: In printing, each picture is broken down into fine dots of the four printing inks. With a magnifying glass you can easily see these halftone dots in a magazine.
111859.m: Printed pictures are made of halftone dots.

111860.q: Where is the CMYK colour model mainly used?
111860.e: Printing presses and inkjet printers put colourings on paper. That is why their colours are described with CMYK.
111860.m: CMYK is the colour model for printing.

111861.q: Why is black printed as well as cyan, magenta and yellow?
a: Because the three colours on top of each other don't give a deep black
Because black is the only waterproof colour
Because paper stays transparent without black
Because black makes the other colours lighter
111861.e: Real printing inks are not perfect, so mixing them often gives only a dark brown or grey. A separate black makes text sharp and saves ink.
111861.m: Printing needs black as a separate ink for deep dark tones.

111862.q: In which unit are CMYK colour values usually given?
111862.e: For each printing ink, the percentage of the area it covers is given. The values range from 0 to 100 per cent.
111862.m: CMYK values are given in per cent.

111863.q: What is the printing process with cyan, magenta, yellow and black called?
111863.e: Magazines and brochures, for example, are printed with these four colours. Their mixtures create a great many shades.
111863.m: Colour pictures are printed with four inks.

111864.q: Why do bright screen colours often look paler when printed?
a: Because CMYK can show fewer bright colours than RGB
Because paper is always slightly yellow
Because the printer lightens colours on purpose
111864.e: The colour range of printing is smaller than that of a screen. So very bright shades such as vivid green or blue can't be printed exactly.
111864.m: Printing can't reproduce all screen colours.

111865.q: What do two complementary colours of light make when mixed additively?
111865.e: Complementary colours of light complete each other to make all parts of white light. So together they make white.
111865.m: Complementary colours of light together make white.

111866.q: In additive mixing, which colour of light is complementary to blue?
111866.e: Yellow light contains exactly the two primary colours that blue lacks. Together all three primary colours are present, and white forms.
111866.m: Blue and yellow light together make white.

111867.q: In additive mixing, which colour of light is complementary to red?
111867.e: Cyan contains exactly the two primary colours that red lacks. Together all three primary colours are present, and white forms.
111867.m: Red light and cyan together make white.

111868.q: In additive mixing, which colour of light is complementary to green?
111868.e: Magenta contains exactly the two primary colours that green lacks. Together all three primary colours are present, and white forms.
111868.m: Green light and magenta together make white.

111869.q: What colour is the afterimage if you stare at a red dot for a long time and then look at a white wall?
111869.e: The red-sensitive cones get tired from staring. On the white wall the signals from the other cones then win, and you see the complementary colour.
111869.m: An afterimage shows the complementary colour.

111870.q: Roughly what do you get if you mix two complementary paints in equal amounts?
111870.e: Together, two complementary colourings absorb almost all visible light. A dark grey or brown forms.
111870.m: Complementary paints mixed together make a dark shade.

111871.q: A grey patch lies on a strong red background. How does the grey look to our eyes?
111871.e: The eye strengthens differences between neighbouring colours. So grey next to red looks slightly tinted with the complementary colour, green.
111871.m: Next to a strong colour, grey looks slightly tinted with the complementary colour.

111872.q: Which pair of colours of light does NOT make white when mixed additively?
111872.e: Red and green don't complete each other to make white, because blue is missing. The other pairs are complementary and make white together.
111872.m: Only complementary colours complete each other to make white.

111873.q: Where does infrared radiation lie compared with visible light?
a: exactly in the middle of the spectrum
111873.e: Infrared joins on to the red end of the visible spectrum. The name means “below red”, referring to the frequency.

111874.q: How do you feel infrared radiation on your skin?
111874.e: Infrared radiation is absorbed by the skin and warms it. That is why you can feel the warmth of a radiator or a fire from a distance.
111874.m: You feel infrared radiation as warmth.

111875.q: Which radiation from the Earth's surface do greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide hold back in the atmosphere?
111875.e: The Earth, warmed by the Sun, gives off heat as infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb part of it and so keep the warmth in the atmosphere.
111875.m: Greenhouse gases hold back infrared radiation.

111876.q: With which measuring instrument did Herschel notice the invisible radiation beyond red light?
111876.e: Herschel placed thermometers in the colours of the spectrum. Beyond the red end the temperature rose even further, although no light could be seen there.
111876.m: Herschel discovered infrared with a thermometer.

111877.q: Which radiation does an ordinary TV remote control use?
111877.e: A small LED in the remote control sends invisible infrared signals. You can often see this flashing with a mobile phone camera.
111877.m: Remote controls send invisible infrared light.

111878.q: What does a thermal imaging camera show?
a: the air pressure in a room
111878.e: Warm objects give off more infrared radiation than cold ones. The camera makes these differences visible as colours.
111878.m: A thermal imaging camera makes infrared radiation visible.

111879.q: Which animals can sense infrared radiation with special pit organs?
111879.e: Pit vipers such as the rattlesnake have pits between the eye and the nostril. With them they sense the heat radiation of prey, even in the dark.
111879.m: Rattlesnakes sense the warmth of their prey.

111880.q: Which radiation does the human body constantly give off because of its body heat?
111880.e: Every warm body gives off heat radiation. At body temperature it is in the infrared range.
111880.m: The human body constantly gives off infrared.

111881.q: Why can't we see infrared radiation?
a: Our eyes are not sensitive to it
111881.e: Our eyes only detect light between violet and red. Infrared lies beyond red, so it is invisible to us.
111881.m: Infrared is invisible to our eyes.

111882.q: Where does ultraviolet radiation lie compared with visible light?
111882.e: Ultraviolet means “beyond violet”. The radiation has a shorter wavelength than violet light and is invisible to humans.

111883.q: What does the UV index in the weather forecast tell you?
a: How strong the Sun's UV radiation is
How warm it will be at midday
How many clouds are in the sky
How strongly the wind is blowing
111883.e: The higher the UV index, the faster you can get sunburnt. When values are high, sun cream, a hat and shade are important.
111883.m: The UV index shows how strong UV radiation is.

111884.q: What can too much UV radiation cause on unprotected skin?
111884.e: UV radiation damages skin cells, and the skin reacts with redness and pain. Frequent sunburn also increases the risk of skin cancer.
111884.m: Too much UV radiation causes sunburn.

111885.q: Which layer of the atmosphere holds back a large part of the Sun's UV radiation?
111885.e: The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere. Ozone molecules absorb a large part of the harmful UV radiation.
111885.m: The ozone layer protects us from UV radiation.

111886.q: Which vitamin does the skin make with the help of UV radiation?
111886.e: UV-B radiation allows the skin to make vitamin D. This vitamin is important for healthy bones.
111886.m: With sunlight, the skin makes vitamin D.

111887.q: Why is UV radiation stronger on a mountain peak in the Alps than in the Swiss Plateau?
a: Because the layer of air above is thinner and filters less UV
Because the Sun is closer there and so bigger
Because rocks produce UV radiation themselves
Because there is no ozone layer in the mountains
111887.e: At altitude the radiation has to pass through less air. Snow also reflects a lot of UV radiation, so sun protection is especially important in the mountains.
111887.m: UV radiation is stronger in the mountains.

111888.q: What happens when UV light hits a highlighter or fluorescent paint?
a: The colour gets hot and melts
111888.e: Fluorescent substances absorb UV radiation and give off visible light. This is how black light works.
111888.m: Under black light, fluorescent colours glow.

111889.q: Into which three ranges is UV radiation divided?
111889.e: The ranges differ in wavelength. UV-A has the longest wavelength, UV-C the shortest and the most energy.
111889.m: UV radiation is divided into UV-A, UV-B and UV-C.

111890.q: Which type of UV radiation hardly reaches the ground at all?
111890.e: The high-energy UV-C radiation is almost completely absorbed in the atmosphere. Most UV-A, on the other hand, reaches the ground.
111890.m: UV-C is almost entirely held back by the atmosphere.

111891.q: Why do clouds look white and not blue like the sky?
a: Their water droplets scatter all colours about equally
They are made of white dust
They absorb all the blue light
111891.e: The droplets in clouds are much larger than air particles. They scatter all colours similarly, and all colours together make white.
111891.m: Clouds scatter all colours equally, so they look white.

111892.q: Which colour of sunlight is scattered especially strongly in all directions by the air?
111892.e: Short-wavelength blue light is scattered much more strongly by air particles than red light. So blue light reaches us from all over the sky.
111892.m: Blue light is scattered most in the air, which is why the sky is blue.

111893.q: Why does the Sun often look reddish when it sets?
a: Because its light takes a long path through the air and the blue is scattered away
Because the Sun cools down in the evening and gives off red light
Because the sea is reflected red in the air
Because the Earth releases heat into the sky in the evening
111893.e: Low on the horizon, sunlight has to pass through much more air. The blue part is scattered to the side, and mainly red and orange light reaches our eyes.
111893.m: Red sunsets happen because blue is lost on the long path through the air.

111894.q: What colour is the sky on Mars around the setting Sun?
111894.e: Fine dust in the Martian atmosphere scatters blue light mainly near the Sun. Photos from Mars rovers therefore show bluish sunsets.

111895.q: Why does the sky look darker blue from a high-flying aeroplane than from the ground?
a: Because there is less air above the plane to scatter light
Because the windows colour the light blue
Because the Sun shines more weakly up there
Because colours no longer exist up there
111895.e: At great height only a small part of the atmosphere is above you. Less light is scattered, and the sky looks darker.
111895.m: The less air above us, the darker the sky looks.

111896.q: Rayleigh scattering is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength. How many times more strongly is light of 400 nm scattered than light of 800 nm?
111896.e: The wavelength is half as large, so the scattering is 2 to the power of 4 times stronger. 2 times 2 times 2 times 2 gives 16.
111896.m: Half the wavelength means sixteen times stronger Rayleigh scattering.

111897.q: Why doesn't the sky look violet, even though violet light is scattered even more strongly?
a: Because the Sun gives off less violet and the eye is less sensitive to it
Because violet light burns up in the air
Because violet light is only scattered at night
Because the clouds absorb all violet light
111897.e: Sunlight contains less violet than blue, and some is absorbed high up in the atmosphere. Our eyes also react more strongly to blue than to violet.
111897.m: Our eyes see the sky as blue instead of violet.

111898.q: What are the cones in the retina mainly responsible for?
111898.e: Cones are sensory cells that react to light of different wavelengths. Working together, they let us tell colours apart.
111898.m: We see colours with our cones.

111899.q: How many types of cones does a person with normal colour vision have?
111899.e: There are cones that react most strongly to red, green or blue light. From their signals the brain puts together all the colours.
111899.m: Humans have three types of cones.

111900.q: What are the sensory cells of the retina called that are mainly responsible for seeing at dusk?
111900.e: Rods are very sensitive to light but cannot tell colours apart. They let us see when there is little light.
111900.m: Rods help us see at dusk.

111901.q: In which layer of the eye are the cones found?
111901.e: The retina lines the inside back of the eye. That is where the sensory cells that turn light into nerve signals sit.
111901.m: The cones are in the retina.

111902.q: What is the spot of sharpest vision called, where there are especially many cones?
111902.e: In the macula, more precisely in the small pit at its centre, the cones are packed very closely. That is where we see most sharply.
111902.m: We see most sharply at the macula.

111903.q: Why can you hardly see colours at night?
a: Because the cones need a lot of light and then hardly work
Because the pupil closes completely at night
Because all objects are grey at night
Because the lens becomes cloudy at night
111903.e: When there is little light, almost only the sensitive rods react. Since they cannot tell colours apart, we see everything in shades of grey.
111903.m: At night we hardly see colours because the cones get too little light.

111904.q: What is different in red-green colour blindness?
a: one type of cone is missing or works differently
111904.e: In red-green colour blindness the red- or green-sensitive cones work differently or are missing. Red and green are then hard to tell apart.
111904.m: Red-green colour blindness is caused by the cones.

111905.q: About how many cones does the retina of a human eye have?
111905.e: One eye has around 6 million cones. Rods are far more numerous, with over 100 million.
111905.m: One eye has a few million cones.

111906.q: How was Newton able to combine the colours of a spectrum back into white light?
a: with a second prism placed the other way round
111906.e: A second prism, turned the other way round, brings the colours back together. Where they meet, white light appears again.
111906.m: Spectral colours can be combined back into white.

111907.q: What happened when Newton sent a single spectral colour through a second prism?
a: It stayed the same and was not split further
It turned back into white light
It broke up into all colours
111907.e: A single spectral colour is bent in the second prism but does not change colour. Newton concluded that the spectral colours are basic.
111907.m: Spectral colours cannot be split any further.

111908.q: What did Newton realise when he sent white light through a prism?
a: White light is a mixture of many colours
White light has no colours at all
111908.e: The prism bends the individual colours by different amounts. This shows that white light contains all the colours of the rainbow.
111908.m: White light is a mixture of many colours.

111909.q: Which colour is bent most strongly by a prism?
111909.e: Violet light is refracted most strongly in glass, red light least. That is why red and violet are at opposite ends of the spectrum.
111909.m: Violet is bent the most, red the least.

111910.q: Which extra colour did Newton include in his spectrum between blue and violet?
111910.e: Indigo is a deep blue-violet. Many experts today no longer see it as a separate spectral colour.
111910.m: Newton counted indigo as a separate spectral colour.

111911.q: Why did Newton choose exactly seven colours for his spectrum?
a: He compared them with the seven notes of the musical scale
He only saw seven colours because of poor eyesight
He took the number of days of the week from the calendar
111911.e: Newton believed in a harmony between colours and music. So he divided the spectrum into seven sections like the musical scale.
111911.m: Newton's seven colours are based on the musical scale.

111912.q: How did Newton arrange the spectral colours to show how they mix?
111912.e: Newton bent the band of colours round into a circle. This let him show which mixed colours come from the individual colours.
111912.m: Newton designed one of the first colour wheels.

111913.q: Which poet criticised Newton and published his own work “Theory of Colours” in 1810?
111913.e: Goethe rejected Newton's explanation of colours and described colours mainly from the point of view of perception. In physics, Newton's view won the day.
111913.m: Goethe set his own theory of colours against Newton's.

111914.q: What does crop rotation mean in the garden?
a: The kinds of plants on a bed change from year to year
You harvest all the fruit in the same week
You plant the same variety in the same place every year
You sow the seeds in one long row
111914.e: With crop rotation, a different crop is grown on the same area each year. This stops the soil from being drained of the same nutrients.
111914.m: With crop rotation, the vegetables change place every year.

111915.q: Why should you not grow cabbage in the same place every year?
a: Diseases and pests build up in the soil
It makes the soil too salty
Otherwise the cabbage only grows downwards
111915.e: If the same plant family is always grown in the same place, its diseases and pests multiply in the soil. This is also called soil sickness.
111915.m: Changing the crops helps prevent diseases in the soil.

111916.q: What do you call vegetables that take a lot of nutrients from the soil, such as pumpkin or cabbage?
111916.e: Heavy feeders need lots of nitrogen and other nutrients. In crop rotation they usually come in the first year after the soil has been fed with compost.
111916.m: Heavy feeders like pumpkin and cabbage need lots of nutrients.

111917.q: Which group of plants are light feeders and even improve the soil?
111917.e: Beans and peas are legumes. They need little fertiliser because bacteria on their roots take nitrogen from the air.
111917.m: Beans and peas are undemanding light feeders.

111918.q: What was the farming method common in the Middle Ages with winter grain, summer grain and fallow land called?
111918.e: In the three-field system, farmland was divided into three parts. One part was always left fallow so that the soil could recover.
111918.m: The three-field system was an early form of crop rotation.

111919.q: What does it mean when a field lies “fallow”?
a: Nothing is planted on it for a while
It is ploughed twice a year
Only grain is grown on it
111919.e: Fallow land is an area that is not used for a time. During this time the soil can recover.
111919.m: On fallow land the soil gets a rest.

111920.q: In a classic three-year vegetable crop rotation, in which order do you change?
a: Heavy feeders, then medium feeders, then light feeders
Light feeders, then heavy feeders, then fallow
Medium feeders, then heavy feeders, then medium feeders
111920.e: After compost has been added, the hungry heavy feeders come first. In the following years come plants that need fewer and fewer nutrients.
111920.m: In crop rotation, heavy feeders come first and light feeders last.

111921.q: Which group are carrots usually put in for crop rotation?
111921.e: Carrots need a medium amount of nutrients. Too much fresh manure even harms them and attracts the carrot fly.

a: Different kinds of plants grow together on one bed
A bed with only one single variety
A mixture of soil and sand
111922.e: In mixed cropping, plants that suit each other are put side by side. They can protect each other from pests and make good use of the space.
111922.m: In mixed cropping, different plants help each other.

111923.q: Which vegetable is often planted next to carrots to confuse the carrot fly?
111923.e: The smell of the onions covers up the smell of the carrots and the other way round. So the carrot fly and onion fly find their host plants less easily.
111923.m: Carrots and onions are good bed neighbours.

111924.q: Which three plants are the “three sisters” of the milpa in Central America?
111924.e: The three plants complement each other: the beans provide nitrogen, and the large squash leaves shade the ground. This mixed cropping is many centuries old.
111924.m: Maize, beans and squash grow together as the three sisters.

111925.q: What does the maize do for the beans in the milpa?
a: It supports them as they climb
111925.e: Climbing beans need something to climb up. The strong maize stalks do this job.
111925.m: The maize stalk is a natural climbing pole for the bean.

111926.q: Which flower is often planted in vegetable beds because it can push back harmful roundworms in the soil?
111926.e: The roots of marigolds (Tagetes) release substances that harm certain roundworms (nematodes). That is why people like to sow them between vegetables.
111926.m: The marigold is a useful flower in the vegetable bed.

111927.q: What is an advantage of deep-rooted and shallow-rooted plants growing next to each other?
a: They use different layers of soil and compete less
They all flower at the same time
They then grow twice as tall
111927.e: Plants with roots of different depths get water and nutrients from different layers. That way they disturb each other less.
111927.m: Different root depths help plants share the soil.

111928.q: Which herb is often planted between tomatoes?
111928.e: Basil and tomatoes have similar needs for warmth and water. The pairing is seen as a classic good neighbourship.
111928.m: Basil is happy next to tomatoes.

111929.q: What is the opposite of mixed cropping, where huge areas are planted with only one kind of plant?
111929.e: In a monoculture, only one kind of plant grows over a large area. Pests can spread more easily there.
111929.m: In a monoculture only one single kind of plant grows.

111930.q: What goes right at the bottom of a classic raised bed?
a: Sand and gravel from the stream
111930.e: A raised bed is filled in layers: coarse wood at the bottom, then leaves and grass cuttings, then compost and soil on top. The coarse branches let air in and water drain away.
111930.m: In a raised bed, coarse material goes at the bottom and fine material on top.

111931.q: Why does a freshly filled raised bed get warmer than a normal bed?
a: The plant remains inside rot and give off heat
The wooden sides glow in the sun
There is a heater at the bottom
The soil contains lots of salt
111931.e: When leaves, grass cuttings and wood rot, heat is produced. That is why you can often sow and harvest earlier in a raised bed.
111931.m: Rotting material warms the raised bed from inside.

111932.q: Why do people often put fine wire mesh on the bottom of a raised bed?
a: So that the water does not drain away
111932.e: Voles like to eat roots and tubers. Fine mesh stops them getting into the raised bed from below.
111932.m: Mesh at the bottom of a raised bed keeps voles out.

111933.q: Which advantage of a raised bed is especially important for older people?
a: You can work without bending down much
You never have to water it
111933.e: The raised working surface is easy on the back. That is why raised beds are also popular in schools and care homes.
111933.m: A raised bed is easy on your back when gardening.

111934.q: Why do you have to top up a raised bed with soil after a few years?
a: Because the filling rots and sinks
Because the plants eat the soil
Because the wind blows the soil away
Because rain turns the soil into stone
111934.e: The plant remains in the lower layers break down over time. This makes the filling sink, and soil is missing at the top.
111934.m: A raised bed sinks over time and needs new soil.

111935.q: Which plants are especially suited to a nutrient-rich raised bed in its first year?
a: Heavy feeders such as courgettes and cabbage
Light feeders such as herbs from the south
111935.e: In its first year a raised bed is very rich in nutrients. Hungry plants such as courgettes, tomatoes or cabbage make good use of this.
111935.m: In a raised bed's first year, hungry vegetables do especially well.

111936.q: What do you need to watch out for with a raised bed in summer?
a: It dries out faster and needs regular watering
You must cover it with snow
You must cut off all the leaves
111936.e: Because a raised bed stands free, sun and wind dry it out faster than a bed in the ground. Mulch helps keep it moist.
111936.m: A raised bed often needs water in summer.

a: Plants you sow to improve the soil
Fertiliser made of green plastic balls
111937.e: With green manure you sow plants not to harvest them, but for the soil. Later they are cut and left as mulch or lightly worked into the soil.
111937.m: Green manure looks after the soil with plants.

111938.q: Which blue-flowered green manure is also called “bee's friend”?
111938.e: Phacelia grows fast, covers the ground and attracts many bees with its flowers. It is not related to most vegetables.
111938.m: Phacelia is known as the bee's friend.

111939.q: Why are clover and lupins especially good as green manure?
a: Bacteria on their roots take nitrogen from the air
They contain lots of iron from stones
111939.e: Clover and lupins are legumes. With the help of bacteria on their roots, they make nitrogen from the air usable for plants.
111939.m: Legumes bring nitrogen into the soil.

111940.q: What do the bacteria in the root nodules of clover and beans give their plant?
111940.e: Nodule bacteria take nitrogen from the air and give it to the plant. In return they get sugar from it. They help each other.
111940.m: Nodule bacteria and legumes help each other.

111941.q: Why is it better not to sow mustard as green manure before cabbage?
a: Both belong to the cabbage family and share diseases
Mustard takes the cabbage's light in winter
111941.e: Mustard and cabbage belong to the cabbage family (crucifers). They can pass on the same diseases, such as clubroot.
111941.m: Related plants should not grow one after the other in the same place.

111942.q: Which danger does green manure reduce on an empty bed in winter?
a: That rain washes the soil away
That the soil gets too warm
That the bed dries out too fast and catches fire
111942.e: Bare soil can be carried away by rain and wind. The plant cover and its roots hold the soil in place.
111942.m: Covered soil is protected from erosion.

111943.q: What is the fertile, dark part of the soil that forms from dead plant remains called?
111943.e: Humus forms when soil creatures break down plant remains. Green manure provides plenty of material for this.
111943.m: Humus makes the soil dark and fertile.

111944.q: What do you normally do with green manure before it forms seeds?
a: You cut it and leave it lying as mulch
You burn it on the bed
You leave it standing for ten years
111944.e: Green manure is mown before the seeds ripen. This way it does not seed itself, and the material can cover and feed the soil.
111944.m: Green manure is mown before the seeds ripen.

a: The seeds grow into the same kind of plants again
111945.e: With open-pollinated varieties, the offspring have the same features as the parent plants. So you can collect your own seeds from them.
111945.m: You can collect your own seeds from open-pollinated varieties.

111946.q: Why is it hardly worth collecting your own seeds from F1 hybrids?
a: The seeds are too small to see
111946.e: F1 hybrids come from crossing two parent lines. In the next generation the features split up and the plants become uneven.
111946.m: F1 hybrids do not produce identical offspring.

111947.q: Why are tomato seeds for saving often left to ferment in their juice for a few days?
a: So that the gel layer that stops sprouting comes off
So that the seeds become sweeter
So that the seeds get bigger
So that the seeds stay red
111947.e: Every tomato seed sits in a slimy coat that stops it from sprouting. Fermenting removes it; afterwards you wash and dry the seeds.
111947.m: Fermented tomato seeds store well and sprout better.

111948.q: Where is the great seed vault in which seeds from all over the world are stored?
111948.e: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault lies in the permafrost on the island of Spitsbergen in Norway. It keeps backup copies of seeds.
111948.m: On Svalbard there is a vault for seeds from all over the world.

111949.q: What is the best way to store seeds?
111949.e: Damp and warmth make seeds go mouldy or age too early. Cool, dry and dark, they stay able to sprout for a long time.
111949.m: Store seeds somewhere cool, dry and dark.

111950.q: What do you call seeds that need light to sprout and are therefore hardly covered with soil?
111950.e: Light germinators such as many kinds of lettuce are only pressed down or covered very thinly. Dark germinators, on the other hand, must be covered with soil.
111950.m: Light germinators need light to sprout.

111951.q: What does the germination rate of seeds tell you?
a: How many seeds can still sprout
How sweet the fruits will be
111951.e: The germination rate is usually given as a percentage. It goes down as the seeds get older.
111951.m: Old seeds often sprout less well than fresh ones.

111952.q: What is the rule of thumb for how deep to sow?
a: About two to three times as deep as the seed is thick
As deep as the spade is long
Always on the surface, whatever the size
111952.e: Small seeds are sown shallow, large seeds deeper. The rule of thumb depends on how thick the seed is.
111952.m: Large seeds are sown deeper than small ones.

111953.q: What is a seedling for planting out?
a: A young plant raised in advance to be planted out
An old plant just before harvest
111953.e: Seedlings are raised in pots or trays. When they are strong enough, they are planted in the bed.
111953.m: A seedling is a young plant that moves into the bed.

111954.q: What is the advantage of seedling pots made of paper or coconut fibre?
a: You can put them in the soil together with the plant
111954.e: The pots break down in the soil. So the roots are not disturbed when planting out.
111954.m: Pots that rot away protect the roots when planting.

111955.q: What does it mean to “harden off” seedlings?
a: Slowly get them used to sun, wind and cold outside
111955.e: Plants from indoors are used to a mild climate. If you first put them outside during the day for a few days, they become tougher.

111956.q: Why can you plant tomato seedlings deeper than they stood in the pot?
a: Extra roots form on the stem
So that the fruits grow underground
So that snails cannot find them
111956.e: Tomatoes grow new roots on the buried part of the stem. The plant then stands more firmly and can take up more water.
111956.m: Tomatoes planted deep grow extra roots.

111957.q: What should you do straight after planting a seedling?
a: Cover it for a week and not water it
111957.e: Watering closes the soil around the roots. This lets the seedling take up water quickly and settle in.
111957.m: Freshly planted plants are watered well.

111958.q: What is the advantage of raising seedlings indoors?
a: The plants get a head start in growing
Afterwards they never need light again
They become immune to all pests
They then produce seeds twice as big
111958.e: In a warm house, plants can already grow while it is still too cold outside. This is important for vegetables that take a long time to ripen, such as peppers.
111958.m: Plants raised early have a head start in the season.

111959.q: Why do seedlings on the windowsill sometimes become long and thin?
111959.e: When there is not enough light, plants stretch out to look for it. This is called etiolation; the stems become weak and pale.
111959.m: Without enough light, young plants grow long and weak.

111960.q: Which plants are usually sown straight into the bed instead of being raised as seedlings?
111960.e: Root vegetables such as carrots do not like being moved, and radishes grow very fast. That is why they are sown directly where they will grow.
111960.m: Carrots and radishes are sown straight into the bed.

111961.q: What does “pricking out” mean in gardening?
a: Moving crowded seedlings so each has more space
Poking plants with needles to make them grow
111961.e: When lots of seedlings are crowded in a tray, you carefully lift them out and plant them one by one in small pots. This gives them room to grow.
111961.m: Pricking out gives young plants more space.

111962.q: When is the right time for pricking out?
a: When the first true leaves appear after the seed leaves
As soon as the seed is in the soil
When the plant has finished flowering
111962.e: The seed leaves often look different from the later leaves. When the first true leaves appear, the little plants are strong enough.
111962.m: You prick out as soon as the first true leaves appear.

111963.q: Which simple tool is often used for pricking out?
111963.e: With a dibber you lift seedlings out of the soil and make planting holes. A pencil or chopstick works too.
111963.m: A dibber helps when moving seedlings.

111964.q: The German gardening word “pikieren” (pricking out) comes from which language?
111964.e: It comes from the French verb “piquer”, which means “to prick”. When pricking out, you poke holes for the little plants.
111964.m: “Pikieren” comes from the French word for prick.

111965.q: Where is the best place to hold a seedling when pricking it out?
a: Not at all, you shake it out
111965.e: The thin stem bends easily and cannot grow back. A seed leaf copes better with a small injury.
111965.m: Hold seedlings by the leaf, not the stem.

111966.q: Why are seedlings that are too crowded pricked out?
a: Otherwise they would take light and space from each other
So that they grow in winter
Because otherwise they get too sweet
111966.e: In a crowded sowing, the little plants compete for light, water and nutrients. When separated, they grow stronger.

111967.q: Which soil is good for sowing and pricking out?
a: Fine seed compost low in nutrients
111967.e: Young plants need loose, fine soil. Few nutrients encourage the roots to grow strongly and search.
111967.m: For seedlings, use loose seed compost with few nutrients.

111968.q: What is meant by biological plant protection?
a: Fighting pests with natural enemies and remedies
111968.e: Biological plant protection relies on helpful creatures, plant extracts and preventive measures. Synthetic chemicals are avoided.
111968.m: Biological plant protection uses nature's helpers.

111969.q: What kind of living thing is Bacillus thuringiensis, which organic farmers use against leaf-eating caterpillars?
111969.e: Bacillus thuringiensis is a bacterium. It makes proteins that are poisonous to certain caterpillars but harmless to people and most other animals.
111969.m: A bacterium helps against hungry caterpillars.

111970.q: Which home-made plant brew is often used against aphids in organic gardens?
111970.e: Nettles are soaked in water and sprayed in diluted form. The brew is meant to drive away aphids and, as a fertiliser, makes the plants stronger.
111970.m: You can make a brew for the garden from nettles.

111971.q: What is a fine insect mesh over a vegetable bed for?
a: It keeps insects such as the cabbage root fly away
It warms the soil like a heater
111971.e: The fine mesh lets light, air and water through. But harmful flies and moths cannot lay their eggs on the plants.
111971.m: A protective mesh keeps harmful insects away physically.

111972.q: Which tiny worms can be added to watering water to fight vine weevil larvae?
111972.e: Certain nematodes (roundworms) get into the larvae and kill them. You buy them from specialist shops and water them in.
111972.m: Helpful nematodes fight beetle larvae in the soil.

111973.q: Which insects are released in greenhouses against whitefly?
111973.e: Parasitic wasps such as Encarsia formosa lay their eggs in whitefly larvae. This makes the larvae die.
111973.m: Parasitic wasps are little helpers against whitefly.

111974.q: What do pheromone traps in the garden use to attract harmful insects?
111974.e: Pheromones are scents that insects use to find each other. The insects that are lured in get stuck in the trap, for example codling moths.
111974.m: Pheromone traps attract insects with scents.

111975.q: Why is healthy, loose soil part of preventive plant protection?
a: Strong plants are less likely to suffer from pests
Because pests cannot see loose soil
111975.e: Well-fed plants grow strongly and can cope better with pests. Prevention is a basic principle of biological plant protection.
111975.m: Healthy plants grow in healthy soil.

111976.q: Which garden creature is known for eating lots of aphids, along with its larvae?
111976.e: Ladybirds, and especially their larvae, eat huge numbers of aphids. They are among the best-known helpful creatures in the garden.
111976.m: The ladybird is a busy aphid hunter.

111977.q: Which larva is called the “aphid lion” because of its appetite for aphids?
a: The caterpillar of the large white butterfly
111977.e: Lacewing larvae grab aphids with their sucking jaws. That is why they have the nickname aphid lion.
111977.m: Lacewing larvae are also called aphid lions.

111978.q: What shelter can you hang in a fruit tree for earwigs?
a: An upside-down flowerpot filled with wood wool
111978.e: During the day, earwigs like to hide in dry hollow spaces. At night they eat aphids, among other things.
111978.m: A pot of wood wool is a hotel for earwigs.

111979.q: Which mammal eats snails, beetles and worms in the garden and hibernates?
111979.e: Hedgehogs hunt insects, snails and other small animals at night. Piles of leaves and branches give them a place to hibernate.
111979.m: The hedgehog is a night-time helper in the garden.

111980.q: Why do people put an insect hotel in the garden?
a: As a nesting place for wild bees and other insects
To catch insects and sell them
As a feeding place for hedgehogs
111980.e: Wild bees in particular lay their eggs in the tubes and holes. Wild bees pollinate many flowers in the garden.
111980.m: An insect hotel gives wild bees a nursery.

111981.q: Which birds are especially helpful because they collect lots of caterpillars for their young?
111981.e: Tits feed their young mainly on insects and caterpillars. A nest box attracts them into the garden.

111982.q: Which flying insects look like small wasps but do not sting, and have larvae that eat aphids?
111982.e: Hoverflies disguise themselves with wasp colours but are harmless. Their larvae eat lots of aphids.

111983.q: Which snake-like animal likes to eat slugs in the garden but is not a snake at all?
111983.e: The slow worm looks like a snake but is a legless lizard. It is harmless and eats slugs and worms.
111983.m: The slow worm is a lizard without legs.

111984.q: Which slug is seen as a particularly annoying pest in Swiss gardens?
111984.e: The Spanish slug does not originally come from Switzerland but probably from western Europe, and it breeds a lot. It often eats young vegetable plants bare overnight.
111984.m: The Spanish slug eats lots of young plants.

111985.q: Which striped beetle eats the leaves of potato plants?
111985.e: The Colorado potato beetle comes from North America and was brought to Europe. It and its red larvae eat potato leaves.
111985.m: The Colorado potato beetle came to Europe from North America.

111986.q: Which sweet substance given off by aphids attracts ants?
111986.e: Aphids suck sugary plant sap and give off the extra as honeydew. Ants protect the aphids so they can collect it.
111986.m: Ants milk aphids for their honeydew.

111987.q: Whose caterpillars eat holes in cabbage leaves?
111987.e: The large white lays its eggs on cabbage plants. The green caterpillars can eat the leaves down to the veins.
111987.m: Large white caterpillars love eating cabbage leaves.

111988.q: Which moth, brought in from East Asia, eats box hedges bare?
111988.e: The box tree moth was brought to Europe and spread quickly. Its caterpillars eat box plants down to the wood.
111988.m: The box tree moth threatens many box hedges.

111989.q: Which rodent eats roots, tubers and flower bulbs underground in the garden?
111989.e: The vole feeds on plants and eats roots and tubers. The mole, on the other hand, eats animals such as earthworms.
111989.m: The vole eats roots, the mole eats worms.

111990.q: Which small fly, brought in from Asia, lays its eggs in ripe cherries and berries?
111990.e: The spotted wing drosophila pierces healthy, ripening fruit and lays eggs there. The fruit then turns mushy.
111990.m: The spotted wing drosophila attacks ripe berries and cherries.

111991.q: How do aphids suck up their food?
a: With a piercing mouthpart from the plant's sap channels
With tiny teeth from the roots
With their feet from the soil
With their wings from the air
111991.e: Aphids pierce the plant with their mouthpart and suck the sap. In doing so they can also spread virus diseases.
111991.m: Aphids suck plant sap with a beak-like mouthpart.

111992.q: Which two English words make up “permaculture”?
111992.e: The term comes from “permanent agriculture”, meaning long-lasting farming. The aim is systems that keep themselves going.

111993.q: In which country did Bill Mollison and David Holmgren develop permaculture in the 1970s?
111993.e: The two Australians published a first book on permaculture in 1978. Since then the idea has spread around the world.

111994.q: In permaculture, what decides how the garden is divided into zones?
a: How often you need to look after and visit an area
The alphabetical order of plant names
111994.e: Areas you use often, such as the herb bed, are close to the house. Areas that need little care, such as the wild area, are further away.
111994.m: In permaculture, the most important things are close to the house.

111995.q: Which idea is at the heart of permaculture?
a: Copying natural cycles and avoiding waste
Buying as much fertiliser as possible
Growing only one single kind of plant
111995.e: Permaculture takes ecosystems such as the forest as its model. Leftovers are used again, for example as compost or mulch.
111995.m: Permaculture copies the cycles of nature.

111996.q: What is a herb spiral, often found in permaculture gardens?
a: A spiral-shaped mound of stones with dry and damp spots
A herbal tea in a spiral shape
111996.e: At the top it is sunny and dry, at the bottom damp and cool. So herbs with different needs find a place in a small space.
111996.m: A herb spiral gives many herbs a place in a small space.

111997.q: Why is the soil covered with mulch in permaculture?
a: It protects against drying out and feeds soil creatures
So that the soil freezes faster
Because mulch turns the plants blue
111997.e: Mulch made of leaves, straw or grass cuttings keeps moisture in the soil. As it rots, it becomes food for soil creatures.
111997.m: Mulch keeps the soil moist and alive.

111998.q: What do you call a garden laid out like a forest in several layers, with trees, shrubs and herbs?
111998.e: A forest garden combines fruit trees, berry bushes, herbs and ground cover. Once it is set up, it needs little care.
111998.m: A forest garden grows in several layers.

111999.q: Why do people like to create a small pond in a permaculture garden?
a: It stores water and gives animals a habitat
So that you can swim in it
Because plants only grow in water
111999.e: A pond holds back rainwater and attracts frogs, dragonflies and birds. These help, for example, against slugs and pests.
111999.m: A pond stores water and brings life to the garden.

112000.q: Who is the German “Schrebergarten” (allotment garden) named after?
112000.e: Moritz Schreber campaigned for exercise in the fresh air. After his death, playgrounds and gardens in Leipzig were named after him.
112000.m: The Schrebergarten is named after a doctor from Leipzig.

112001.q: What are allotment gardens usually called in Switzerland?
112001.e: In Switzerland people usually speak of family gardens. They are often leased out by clubs on land owned by the municipality.
112001.m: In Switzerland, allotments are often called family gardens.

112002.q: What was the plan called with which Switzerland grew much more of its own food in the Second World War, even on sports fields and in parks?
112002.e: The Cultivation Battle (Anbauschlacht) is also called the Wahlen Plan after its creator, Friedrich Traugott Wahlen. At that time vegetables were also grown in many family gardens and allotments in the cities.
112002.m: In the Cultivation Battle, Switzerland planted vegetables and potatoes everywhere.

112003.q: Why did allotment gardens appear in the growing cities of the 19th century?
a: Working families were meant to have a place to relax and their own vegetables
112003.e: Cramped city flats lacked greenery. A small garden offered fresh air, exercise and extra food.
112003.m: Allotments brought greenery and vegetables into the cities.

112004.q: Who usually gives out an allotment garden?
a: A club that leases out the plots
112004.e: Allotments are usually organised in clubs. You lease a plot and must follow the garden rules.
112004.m: You usually lease an allotment from a club.

112005.q: What do you call a single piece of garden in an allotment site?
112005.e: An allotment site is divided into many plots. Each plot is leased by one person or family.
112005.m: An allotment is a plot on a garden site.

112006.q: What small hut for tools stands in many allotment gardens?
112006.e: The garden shed is used as a shelter and a store for tools. Living in it is usually not allowed.
112006.m: Garden tools are kept in the garden shed.

112007.q: What do many sets of rules for family gardens require?
a: That part of the area is used for vegetables, fruit or flowers
That the whole garden is concreted over
That a swimming pool is built every year
112007.e: Family gardens are meant for growing things, not just for leisure. That is why clubs often set rules on how the area is used.
112007.m: A family garden is mainly there for gardening.

112008.q: Which types of wood are especially good for the sides of a raised bed?
112008.e: Larch and Douglas fir wood contain lots of resin and resist damp for a long time. That is why they rot more slowly than other woods.
112008.m: Wood rich in resin lasts longer in a raised bed.

112009.q: Where should you put little plants that have just been pricked out?
a: Somewhere bright, but not in full sun
112009.e: After being moved, the roots first have to settle in again. Full sun would dry the little plants out during this time.
112009.m: Pricked-out plants need light but protection from full sun.

112010.q: Why should potatoes not grow straight after tomatoes in the same place?
a: Both are nightshades with the same diseases
Tomatoes make the soil too acidic for tubers
Tomato roots grow into the potatoes
112010.e: Potatoes and tomatoes belong to the same plant family. Diseases such as late blight attack both.
112010.m: Related vegetables should not follow each other in crop rotation.

112011.q: Which beetles, usually dark and shiny, hunt snails and insects on the ground at night?
112011.e: Ground beetles are quick hunters. Many species eat slug eggs, small slugs and insect larvae.
112011.m: Ground beetles are night-time hunters in the garden soil.

a: A paper strip with seeds at the right spacing
A rubber band for seed packets
112012.e: In seed tape, the seeds are already set at the right distances. You lay it in the seed drill and cover it with soil.
112012.m: Seed tape makes it easier to sow at even distances.

112013.q: Which plant brew is sprayed in organic gardens to prevent fungal diseases?
112013.e: Field horsetail contains lots of silica. The brew is meant to strengthen the leaf surface and make it harder for fungi to get in.
112013.m: Horsetail brew makes plants stronger against fungi.

112014.q: What mainly drives the currents at the surface of the sea?
112014.e: Steady winds such as the trade winds push the surface water along in front of them. This creates large currents at the surface.
112014.m: Surface currents are mainly driven by the wind.

112015.q: What drives the big currents deep in the oceans?
a: Differences in temperature and salt content
112015.e: Cold, salty water is heavier and sinks, while warmer water rises. This current links all the oceans like a giant conveyor belt; experts call it thermohaline circulation.
112015.m: Heat and salt move the water deep in the oceans.

112016.q: Why does cold, salty seawater sink to the depths?
a: It is lighter than warm water
It is pulled down by fish
112016.e: The colder and saltier water is, the denser and heavier it is. That is why it sinks below warmer water with less salt.
112016.m: Cold, salty water is heavier and sinks.

112017.q: Which ocean current flows around Antarctica and is the one carrying the most water in the world?
112017.e: This current flows all the way around Antarctica without being blocked by continents. It carries more water than any other ocean current.
112017.m: The biggest ocean current flows around Antarctica.

112018.q: What deflects big ocean currents and winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere?
112018.e: Because the Earth turns, moving masses of water and air are deflected: to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. Experts call this the Coriolis force.
112018.m: The Earth's rotation deflects ocean currents.

112019.q: What are the huge circular current systems in the oceans called, where plastic rubbish also collects?
112019.e: In the big ocean basins, currents circle in huge loops. Floating debris collects in the middle, for example in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.
112019.m: Floating rubbish collects in ocean gyres.

112020.q: Which weather event in the Pacific happens when the currents change and the water off Peru becomes unusually warm?
112020.e: During El Niño, the trade winds weaken and warm water spreads east. This changes the weather in many parts of the world.
112020.m: El Niño brings unusually warm water off South America.

112021.q: Where does the Gulf Stream get its name from?
112021.e: The Gulf Stream starts in the area of the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean. From there it flows north along the east coast of North America.
112021.m: The Gulf Stream is named after the Gulf of Mexico.

112022.q: What effect does the Gulf Stream, with its extension the North Atlantic Current, have on Europe?
a: It makes the winters much colder
112022.e: The current brings warm water from the tropics to northern Europe. That is why it is much milder there than in other places at the same latitude.
112022.m: The Gulf Stream works like central heating for Europe.

112023.q: Which harbours usually stay free of ice in winter thanks to the warm current, even though they lie north of the Arctic Circle?
a: Harbours on the coast of Norway
112023.e: The warm water of the North Atlantic Current flows right up to the Norwegian coast. That is why harbours such as Hammerfest do not freeze over in winter.
112023.m: Thanks to warm Atlantic water, Norway's harbours do not freeze.

112024.q: Which American statesman had a map of the Gulf Stream printed in the 18th century?
112024.e: Franklin was in charge of the post in the British colonies. He wanted to know why mail ships from England to America were slower than merchant ships, and had the Gulf Stream mapped with the help of sailors.
112024.m: Benjamin Franklin drew an early map of the Gulf Stream.

112025.q: Is the Gulf Stream a warm or a cold ocean current?
112025.e: The Gulf Stream carries warm water from the tropics northwards. Its temperature is much higher than that of the surrounding water.
112025.m: The Gulf Stream brings warm water north.

112026.q: Why are researchers watching the current system in the Atlantic, which the Gulf Stream belongs to, in connection with climate change?
a: Meltwater could weaken the overturning circulation
The Gulf Stream could freeze into ice
The Gulf Stream could move to the Pacific
The Gulf Stream could become salty
112026.e: A lot of fresh water from melting ice makes the seawater lighter, so it sinks less strongly. This could weaken the great overturning circulation in the Atlantic.
112026.m: Meltwater can change the ocean currents in the Atlantic.

112027.q: Along which coast does the Gulf Stream flow from south to north?
a: Along the east coast of North America
Along the west coast of Africa
112027.e: From Florida, the Gulf Stream flows north along the east coast of the USA. After that it turns across the Atlantic towards Europe.
112027.m: The Gulf Stream runs along the east coast of North America.

112028.q: What do you call an especially high tide at full moon or new moon?
112028.e: At full moon and new moon, the sun, moon and Earth are in a line. Their pulling forces add together, so the tides are stronger.
112028.m: At full moon and new moon, the tides are especially strong.

112029.q: At which phase of the moon are the tides especially weak?
112029.e: At half moon, the sun and moon pull at right angles to each other. Their forces partly cancel each other out.
112029.m: At half moon, the tides are weak.

112030.q: Where is the difference between high and low tide the biggest in the world, at up to about 16 metres?
a: In the Bay of Fundy in Canada
In the Baltic Sea near Kiel
112030.e: In the Bay of Fundy, the water in the narrow bay sloshes back and forth especially strongly. The difference between high and low tide there is huge.
112030.m: In the Bay of Fundy, the sea rises and falls the most.

112031.q: In which country is one of the world's first big tidal power stations, at the mouth of the Rance?
112031.e: The tidal power station on the Rance in Brittany started working in 1966. Turbines there use the water flowing in and out.
112031.m: Tidal power stations make electricity from the tides.

112032.q: Roughly how deep is the Mariana Trench at its deepest point?
112032.e: The deepest point is called the Challenger Deep and lies almost 11 kilometres below sea level. Mount Everest would disappear completely inside it.
112032.m: The Mariana Trench is almost 11 kilometres deep.

112033.q: Which small crustaceans have even been found at the bottom of the Mariana Trench?
112033.e: Samples and cameras showed that amphipods live at the bottom of the trench. They feed on scraps that sink down from above.
112033.m: There is life even at the greatest depths of the sea.

112034.q: Which film director dived alone in a submersible to the bottom of the Mariana Trench in 2012?
112034.e: James Cameron was the first person to reach the deepest point of the trench alone in his submersible. He is known for films such as “Titanic”.
112034.m: James Cameron dived alone into the deepest trench on Earth.

112035.q: How does water pressure change the deeper you dive in the sea?
112035.e: For every 10 metres of depth, the pressure rises by about 1 bar. At the bottom of the Mariana Trench, it is more than a thousand times greater than at the surface.
112035.m: The deeper you dive, the greater the water pressure.

112036.q: Which Swiss physicist designed the bathyscaphe “Trieste”?
112036.e: Auguste Piccard had earlier gone up into the stratosphere in a balloon. After that he built submersibles for the deep sea, including the “Trieste”; his son Jacques later piloted it.
112036.m: Auguste Piccard invented submersibles for the deep sea.

112037.q: What does the Greek word “bathyscaphe” roughly mean?
112037.e: “Bathys” means deep and “skaphos” means ship. So a bathyscaphe is a deep-sea ship.
112037.m: A bathyscaphe is a ship for the deep.

112038.q: What was the big float of the “Trieste” filled with so that it would have buoyancy?
112038.e: Petrol is lighter than water and can hardly be squeezed. That is why it gave buoyancy even under high pressure.
112038.m: The “Trieste” floated in the water thanks to petrol.

112039.q: How could the “Trieste” come back up after a dive?
a: It dropped iron pellets used as ballast
A ship pulled it up on a rope
It went straight up with propellers
112039.e: Iron shot kept the “Trieste” heavy on the way down. When it was dropped, the boat was lighter than water and rose.
112039.m: Dropping ballast makes a submersible rise.

112040.q: Which city was the “Trieste” named after?
112040.e: Large parts of the “Trieste” were built in Trieste, and the city supported the project. In 1953 it was first launched in Italy, near Naples.
112040.m: The “Trieste” is named after an Italian port city.

112041.q: Where did the crew of the “Trieste” sit during a dive?
a: In a small steel sphere under the float
In a wooden hut on the roof
112041.e: The crew sat in a thick-walled steel pressure sphere. Only this could withstand the enormous water pressure.
112041.m: A steel pressure sphere protected the divers of the “Trieste”.

112042.q: How does sonar measure the depth of the sea?
a: With sound waves and their echo
112042.e: Sonar sends out pulses of sound and measures how long the echo takes to come back from the seabed. From this it calculates the distance.
112042.m: Sonar measures distances using the echo of sound.

112043.q: Roughly how fast does sound travel in seawater?
112043.e: In water, sound is about four times faster than in air. The exact value depends on temperature, salt content and pressure.
112043.m: Sound is much faster in water than in air.

112044.q: An echo sounder picks up the echo after 2 seconds. How deep is the sea if sound travels at 1500 m/s?
112044.e: In 2 seconds, the sound travels 3000 metres, but that is there and back. So the depth is 3000 divided by 2, which gives 1500 metres.
112044.m: With an echo sounder, you divide the distance by two because the sound goes there and back.

112045.q: What is the device on ships called that uses sound to measure the depth of water under the ship?
112045.e: The echo sounder is a simple form of sonar. It sends sound straight down and measures the time until the echo returns.
112045.m: An echo sounder measures the water depth under the ship.

112046.q: Which sea animals find their way with echoes, a bit like sonar?
112046.e: Dolphins make clicking sounds and listen for the echo. That is how they find prey and obstacles, even in murky water.
112046.m: Dolphins see with their ears by using echoes.

112047.q: What does the English abbreviation “sonar” stand for?
112047.e: The name means navigating and measuring distances with sound. A similar idea that uses radio waves is radar.
112047.m: Sonar works with sound, radar with radio waves.

112048.q: Which shipwreck in 1912 sped up the development of devices that use sound to find obstacles under water?
112048.e: The Titanic sank after hitting an iceberg. Afterwards, people looked for ways to detect icebergs and obstacles with sound in good time.
112048.m: After the Titanic disaster, detection with sound was pushed forward.

112049.q: What do researchers use modern multibeam echo sounders for today?
a: To make maps of the seabed
To take the salt out of water
112049.e: A multibeam echo sounder sends out many beams of sound at once in a wide strip. Bit by bit, this builds an accurate picture of the seabed.
112049.m: Researchers map the seabed with sound.

112050.q: Which tiny animals build a coral reef?
112050.e: Coral polyps are small animals related to jellyfish. They give off limestone, from which huge reefs grow over a very long time.
112050.m: Tiny coral polyps build huge reefs out of limestone.

112051.q: Off which country does the Great Barrier Reef lie?
112051.e: The Great Barrier Reef lies off the north-east coast of Australia. It is the largest coral reef in the world and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
112051.m: The Great Barrier Reef lies off Australia.

112052.q: What happens to corals when the seawater gets too warm?
112052.e: When the water is too warm, corals push out the tiny algae that give them colour and food. They turn white and can die.
112052.m: Water that is too warm makes corals bleach.

112053.q: Which fish is the largest in the world but still feeds mainly on plankton?
112053.e: The whale shark can grow to more than 12 metres long. It filters plankton and small fish out of the water.
112053.m: The whale shark is a giant plankton eater.

112054.q: What causes the “glowing sea” on some coasts at night?
112054.e: Certain single-celled creatures such as Noctiluca glow when the water moves. Making light like this is called bioluminescence.
112054.m: Glowing plankton makes waves sparkle at night.

112055.q: Why is plankton the basis of the food chain in the sea?
a: Almost all sea animals depend on it directly or indirectly
Because it is only eaten by sharks
Because it only lives in fresh water
112055.e: Phytoplankton makes food from sunlight, zooplankton eats it, and small fish eat the zooplankton. Larger animals build on this.
112055.m: Without plankton there would be hardly any life in the sea.

112056.q: Roughly what is the average salt content of the oceans?
112056.e: On average, one kilogram of seawater contains about 35 grams of dissolved salts. That is about 3.5 per cent.
112056.m: On average, seawater contains about 3.5 per cent salt.

112057.q: Which salt is the most common in seawater?
112057.e: The chemical name for table salt is sodium chloride. It makes up most of the salts in the sea.
112057.m: Most of the salt in the sea is table salt.

112058.q: Why is the Baltic Sea much less salty than the open Atlantic?
a: Many rivers bring fresh water, and the link to the North Sea is narrow
Because a lot of water evaporates there
Because fish eat the salt out of the water
Because the Baltic Sea has no seabed
112058.e: Many big rivers flow into the Baltic Sea, and more rain falls than evaporates. Salty North Sea water only gets in through narrow straits near Denmark.
112058.m: The Baltic Sea contains much less salt than the Atlantic.

112059.q: How can you get drinking water from seawater?
a: By desalination, for example by evaporating or filtering
112059.e: Desalination plants evaporate the water or press it through very fine membranes. The salt is left behind.
112059.m: Seawater has to be desalinated before you can drink it.

112060.q: What are Argo floats, which today add to the measurements from research ships?
a: Drifting measuring robots that dive and rise on their own
112060.e: Thousands of these devices drift in all the oceans. They measure temperature and salt content and send the data by satellite.
112060.m: Measuring robots send data from all the oceans.

112061.q: What did Jacques-Yves Cousteau explore with his ship “Calypso”?
112061.e: Cousteau turned an old minesweeper into a floating laboratory. With his films he showed many people the underwater world.
112061.m: Cousteau explored the seas with the “Calypso”.

112062.q: In which ship did Fridtjof Nansen drift through the Arctic Ocean in the pack ice in 1893?
112062.e: The “Fram” was built so that the ice would push it upwards instead of crushing it. In this way, Nansen wanted to study the current in the Arctic Ocean.
112062.m: The “Fram” drifted with the ice across the Arctic Ocean.

112063.q: What do research ships need a device called a CTD probe for?
a: To measure conductivity, temperature and depth
112063.e: CTD stands for Conductivity, Temperature and Depth. From the water's conductivity, the salt content can be calculated.
112063.m: A CTD probe measures salt, heat and depth in the sea.

112064.q: What is an ROV, which is used from many research ships?
112064.e: ROV stands for Remotely Operated Vehicle. It hangs on a cable and is controlled from the ship to explore the deep with cameras and gripping arms.
112064.m: Underwater robots explore the deep sea for researchers.

112065.q: Why do research ships use long pipes to take cores from the seabed?
a: The layers reveal something about the climate of the past
To fill up with oil there
112065.e: In the mud on the seabed, layers build up over a very long time. They contain the remains of living things, which give clues about earlier climates.
112065.m: Cores from the seabed are an archive of Earth's history.

112066.q: In which vehicle can researchers go down into the deep sea themselves?
112066.e: Submersibles have a thick hull that withstands the water pressure. In 1986, the submersible “Alvin” even visited the wreck of the Titanic.
112066.m: Researchers reach the deep sea in submersibles.

112067.q: Where do hydrothermal vents usually form?
a: At mid-ocean ridges, where tectonic plates drift apart
112067.e: At the ridges, seawater seeps into cracks, is heated by magma and rises again. This creates hot springs on the seabed.
112067.m: Hydrothermal vents are often found at mid-ocean ridges.

112068.q: What is the process called in which bacteria at hydrothermal vents make food without sunlight?
112068.e: The bacteria get energy from chemicals in the vent water. They use it to make sugar, without any light at all.
112068.m: In the dark deep sea, food is made by chemosynthesis.

112069.q: What do scientists use to explore hydrothermal vents in the deep sea?
112069.e: The vents are often more than 2000 metres deep. Only special submersibles and robots can withstand the huge water pressure.
112069.m: The deep sea is explored with submersibles.

112070.q: Which animals, more than two metres long with red plumes, live at hydrothermal vents?
112070.e: Giant tube worms have no mouth and no gut. Bacteria live inside their bodies and supply them with food.
112070.m: Giant tube worms live off bacteria inside their bodies.

112071.q: Why does the water at black smokers, which is over 300 degrees, not boil?
a: The high water pressure stops it boiling
The water is too salty to boil
Because there is no fire there
112071.e: The higher the pressure, the higher the boiling point of water. Deep down, the water therefore stays liquid despite the heat.
112071.m: High pressure raises the boiling point of water.

112072.q: Why are researchers at hydrothermal vents interested in how life began?
a: The first life on Earth may have formed there
112072.e: At the vents there is heat, energy and lots of chemicals. Some researchers think the first cells formed there billions of years ago.
112072.m: Deep-sea vents could be the cradle of life.

112073.q: Which raw materials build up at hydrothermal vents and attract interest from deep-sea mining?
a: Metals such as copper and zinc
112073.e: Metal sulphides come out of the hot water and form ore deposits. Mining them is controversial because it could destroy rare habitats.
112073.m: Metal-rich ores form at deep-sea vents.

112074.q: Which diving device did Cousteau develop in 1943 together with Émile Gagnan?
112074.e: The Aqualung supplied air from compressed air tanks, but only when the diver breathed in. This made free diving much easier.
112074.m: The Aqualung made scuba diving possible.

112075.q: How did Cousteau show many people the world under water?
112075.e: Cousteau made many documentary films and television series. His film “The Silent World” won the Palme d'Or at Cannes in 1956.
112075.m: Cousteau showed the underwater world in films.

112076.q: Which item of clothing became Cousteau's trademark?
112076.e: Cousteau and his crew often wore red woollen caps. The cap became his best-known trademark.
112076.m: You can recognise Cousteau by his red cap.

112077.q: What did Cousteau test with his “Conshelf” projects in the 1960s?
a: Whether people can live in underwater stations for a long time
Whether you can dive on the moon
Whether ships can sail without an engine
112077.e: In the Conshelf stations, divers lived under water for several days or weeks. They wanted to show that people can work on the seabed.
112077.m: Cousteau had people live in houses under water.

112078.q: What did Cousteau especially campaign for in his later years?
112078.e: Cousteau saw how pollution and overfishing were harming the oceans. He founded an organisation that works for the oceans.
112078.m: Cousteau fought for clean, healthy seas.

112079.q: What job did Cousteau have before he became famous as an ocean explorer?
112079.e: Cousteau joined the French Navy as a young man. Because he was no longer allowed to fly after a car accident, he started diving.
112079.m: Cousteau came to diving through the navy.
